Messages.Author: atomweaver
Messages.Body:
Peter D Bakija <pd...@lightlink.com> wrote in
news:pdb6-75BF51.1...@news-server.stny.rr.com:

> That Voter Cap just lets you virtually
> instantly refill your vampire for, like, nothing, all while hurting
> your prey at the same time is likely the issue here.
>

Recognizing that this only occurs after you've invested mondo-pool into
a large capacity minion, possibly two, survived the big red combat
target such a minion comes pre-installed with, and the faster weenie
bleed decks that have pushed your pool dangerously low ('cause your
large caps cost more initial investment), have taken a political action
without getting blocked by the wall deck, gotten to the referendum, not
had another political deck (or more) at the table voting against, have
the available space on the minion due to a Minion Tap which was deep
enough, but not too deep, got the Awe in your opening draw, and have
enough overkill vote to refill, and not have the whole thing DT'ed
post-Awe... in other words, like, nothing.

It seems like you've convinced yourself that VC is a problem, but I'm
not seeing it. VC is one of the few cards that adequately rewards the
risk associated with large capacity minions, and does it in a manner
where the effect scales down to smaller vampires appropriately. The
other thing about its effect is that a host of other, common competitive
decks can interfere with VC's end result, merely by them "doing their
thing" properly. Even without the common DT defense, wall decks, combat
decks, and bleed decks adjacent to a vote deck create an environment
where a large cap vote deck cannot just "do its thing", as you've been
arguing here. The wall deck intercepts the vote, the combat deck kills
the PRE vamp before it can act, the bleed deck leans into it hard and
fast, because the player has risked more pool on a bigger vampire. If
bleed, wall, and combat concepts can all already deal effectively with a
bloat tactic, without going out of their way in terms of deck-builiding,
why does anything vote-related need to be changed?

Once in a while a big-cap PRE deck gets its game on at the right
table, and you hear about a guy ending the game with a sweep and 78
pool in the kitty. *shrug* So what? Weird things happen when many
games get played. Ahrimanes win the EC... Assamites win a Storyline.
As often as not, if I see a Pre vote deck winning, its doing so by
the skin of its teeth, and needs what bloat it can get from VC to stay
in the game. I'm not hearing much about the overwhelming success of
big-cap PRE vote decks on the tournament scene, either... and if
you're arguing "overpowered", then I've gotta see some proof of that
before I can get behind any change, (and also know that the proof is
that VC is the issue, and not, say, Arika or PTO.)

Regards,
DaveZ
Atom Weaver

On Feb 7, 9:19 am, atomweaver <atomwea...@hotmail.com> wrote:
> It seems like you've convinced yourself that VC is a problem, but I'm

Nah. I haven't convinced myself it is a problem. I have convinced
myself that it *might* be a problem. And I have also convinced myself
that it does hinder the design team significantly in making new vote
cards.

As noted, aside from limiting the ability to add blood/pool costs to
vote cards, it is possible that Voter Cap alone is keeping the vote
strategy as a whole totally stagnant--because Voter Cap is as powerful
as it is (I think we can at least all agree that Voter Cap is
certainly powerful), it is certainly possible that the design team is
holding back new and exciting vote strategies and abilities on the
grounds of "Well, with Voter Cap, this is already on the top of the
power curve". This is supposition, yes. But certainly possible.

Like, yeah, it is possible that downpowering Voter Cap could be
hindersome to some vote decks. But by doing so, there would be a lot
of new avenues for new cards to rebolster those decks. For an obvious
example, with Voter Cap nerfed, why not introduce a Political Action
that did the same thing (i.e. gave you blood and/or pool based on how
many votes you passed the referendum by)? This would be a perfectly
reasonable card. And then combined with the downpowered Voter Cap
would produce a great deal of bloat possibility while, like most of
the other cards that do a similar thing, happen in and of themselves
instead of doing so while also making your prey lose 4 pool.

> and if you're arguing "overpowered", then I've gotta see some proof of that
> before I can get behind any change

Any "overpowered" that I am refering to is solely in comparison to
cards that do similar things (5th Tradition, Giant's Blood, Taste,
Entenching, Concert Tour, etc.) Which, a lot of the time, is exactly
where one locates overpoweredness.

-Peter

> viability of large-cap vote decks, and large-cap decks are usually too

That is certainly a possibility. But then again, it might also open up
interesting ways to re-increase the viability of large cap vote decks.

Like, I totally understand that some folks don't want to see the card
changed for completely practical reasons--they don't want all those
Voter Caps in circulation to suddenly become wallpaper, which confuses
new players and irritates old ones.

And I also totally understand that some folks don't want to see the
card changed because it will make large vampire vote decks less
effective to some level.

But on an absolute design level, assuming that the first is not an
issue at all (which is a big assumption, I know) and that the second
is something that could easily be addressed by new cards, the fixing
of Voter Cap strikes me as a totally sound idea.

But I know that the first issue is a problem. And the second is one
that would take a long time to re-adjust. Which is why, in reality, I
am totally ok one way or the other. Regardless of the fervor with
which I post.

-Peter

fifth tradition. Maybe they should consider giving other deck types
better bloating capabilities instead? I would say introducing more
effective/interesting cards is a better idea than fixing old ones.

Messages.Author: Peter D Bakija
Messages.Body:
On Feb 7, 10:45 am, atomweaver <atomwea...@hotmail.com> wrote:
> The other thing I really want card change advocates (be it VC, or any other
> card) to think about is, is the problem big enough to warrant changing a
> card's text, in light of the extra burden that adds to new players?

I addressed this point in another post (I realize it is difficult, if
not impossible, to keep track of all my ramblings :-)--here is the
thing. At least for me. I completely realize that this is a totally
significant issue.But it is also one that I tend to ignore when
discussing design issues. 'Cause at least from my perspective, I'm
always willing to suck up errata/new card text in the name of making
the game work better. For my money, making the game better will
*always* trump the inconvinience of errata. But I fully realize that
that is just me.

So while I in no way deny that this is a significant issue, it is not
one that I, personally, tend to worry about. And as such, I don't
factor it into my discussion. That being said, yeah, it is a huge pain
to have cards that don't have the right text, and it is a problem for
newer players.

> If its a big enough problem, it better be big enough to be banned, IMO.

If I thought that was the only viable option (which it might very well
be), I'd be totally ok with that (i.e. banning Voter Captivation and
the immediately introducing Bloater Blaptivation that had the fixed
Voter Cap text on it). But in reality, I suspect that most folks would
rather all their old Voter Cap cards be useable, even if they have to
remember errata, then have all their old Voter Caps get banned and
then have to replace them all. But I could be wrong.

-Peter

Messages.Author: atomweaver
Messages.Body:
"Peter D Bakija" <pd...@lightlink.com> wrote in

news:1170866246.1...@a34g2000cwb.googlegroups.com:

> On Feb 7, 10:45 am, atomweaver <atomwea...@hotmail.com> wrote:
>> The other thing I really want card change advocates (be it VC, or any
>> other card) to think about is, is the problem big enough to warrant
>> changing a card's text, in light of the extra burden that adds to new
>> players?
>
> I addressed this point in another post (I realize it is difficult, if
> not impossible, to keep track of all my ramblings :-)--here is the
> thing. At least for me. I completely realize that this is a totally
> significant issue.But it is also one that I tend to ignore when
> discussing design issues.

Well, that's fine if you're Joe Player... But if you're on the Design
Team, or if you're advocating yet more Stuff that new players need to be
aware of, I'd appreciate considering the extra burden it puts on guys like
me.

At first I thought that re-writes would be a boon, and in some cases they
are. Horribly horrible cards which really needed to be reigned in can
remain a part of the game. After the list got over 100 cards long, though,
it really puts a big obstacle in the way of devloping a new player base.
You'd like to think that most recent printing (MRP) is nice, but if I'm
setting up a new group, I'm mostly using my own cards. If i want to use
MRP with old cards, I've got to teach the relevant parts of the migration
list to the new players, anyways. I'm fine with doing that for, say,
Majesty, which was singlehandedly keeping Good Combat down. I'm not fine
with doing it for purpose of eliminating the cost of Wasserschloss Anif,
Austria, which still doesn't see any play, and about 50 to 70% of the other
card text migrations.

> 'Cause at least from my perspective, I'm
> always willing to suck up errata/new card text in the name of making
> the game work better. For my money, making the game better will
> *always* trump the inconvinience of errata. But I fully realize that
> that is just me.
>

Yuck. That attitude would result in killing the game off by inches, one
card at a time, IMO. There's always going to be some imbalance in the
game... it wouldn't be interesting to play if there weren't.

> So while I in no way deny that this is a significant issue, it is not
> one that I, personally, tend to worry about. And as such, I don't
> factor it into my discussion. That being said, yeah, it is a huge pain
> to have cards that don't have the right text, and it is a problem for
> newer players.
>
>> If its a big enough problem, it better be big enough to be banned,
>> IMO.
>
> If I thought that was the only viable option (which it might very well
> be), I'd be totally ok with that (i.e. banning Voter Captivation and
> the immediately introducing Bloater Blaptivation that had the fixed
> Voter Cap text on it). But in reality, I suspect that most folks would
> rather all their old Voter Cap cards be useable, even if they have to
> remember errata, then have all their old Voter Caps get banned and
> then have to replace them all. But I could be wrong.
>

I used to think that playing with old cards would be preferred, and it
would be, _if_ the migration list were kept short (and finite)... but
dealing with the wealth of older cards in the presence of new players is
already a gigantic pain, and that problem does nothing but grow as more
cards get functional changes. This game has enough trouble attracting new
players, as it is.

DZ
AW

Messages.Author: Robert Goudie
Messages.Body:
On Feb 7, 7:45 am, atomweaver <atomwea...@hotmail.com> wrote:

> "Peter D Bakija" <p...@lightlink.com> wrote innews:1170859209.8...@a75g2000cwd.googlegroups.com:
>
> > On Feb 7, 9:19 am, atomweaver <atomwea...@hotmail.com> wrote:
> >> It seems like you've convinced yourself that VC is a problem, but I'm
> >> not seeing it.
>
> > Nah. I haven't convinced myself it is a problem. I have convinced
> > myself that it *might* be a problem. And I have also convinced myself
> > that it does hinder the design team significantly in making new vote
> > cards.
>
> The other thing I really want card change advocates (be it VC, or any other
> card) to think about is, is the problem big enough to warrant changing a
> card's text, in light of the extra burden that adds to new players?

New Card Text is an inconvenience for existing players but shouldn't
be an issue for new players. New players are purchasing new cards with
the new text on them so they're hardly confused. Errata is the thing
that we need to have as little of as possible because it negatively
affects existing players and new players alike.

> Personally, I've got a fairly high threshold for changing text. That
> mostly stems from how often i have to introduce the game to new players.
> On the back end of the many changes to card text, I can say it is _not_the
> blessing I thought it was five years ago. Its just another set of
> problems/complications that need to be clarified, which is why I'd rather
> we would all just be done with meddling with card text, altogether.

Yeah, in practical terms I know the people I've taught have often been
taught with crap from my old piles of common cards. And then I give
them lots of old Jyhad cards too. So, yes, that's a bummer since there
are lots of changes. I try to stick to the new starter decks and base
sets for teaching now.

-Robert

Messages.Author: atomweaver
Messages.Body:
"Robert Goudie" <rob...@vtesinla.org> wrote in
news:1170869460.9...@s48g2000cws.googlegroups.com:

> New Card Text is an inconvenience for existing players but shouldn't
> be an issue for new players. New players are purchasing new cards with
> the new text on them so they're hardly confused. Errata is the thing
> that we need to have as little of as possible because it negatively
> affects existing players and new players alike.
>

I'll give you a super-common scenario; an Old Player meets/plays
against a New Player, and Old Player is playing his old cards... He
plays something New Player hasn't seen before. New Player askes "can I
read that?". Old player answers "Yeah, but it doesn't work as written",
and so needs to explain to New Player anyways. The burden on ease of
play isn't as great as errata, but its still a burden.

>
> Yeah, in practical terms I know the people I've taught have often been
> taught with crap from my old piles of common cards. And then I give
> them lots of old Jyhad cards too. So, yes, that's a bummer since there
> are lots of changes. I try to stick to the new starter decks and base
> sets for teaching now.
>

...and I make people buy the Player's Kit at Barnes and Noble :-) But
really, if we aren't going to put a lid on re-wording cards, a problem
which is mostly an issue for old players playing old cards with new
players (ie, my problem) will eventually become a problem everybody will
have to deal with on a regular basis. I'm just letting you know
firsthand, from this side of the issue, its a big pain in the ass.

From this perspective, I'm saying if something is decided to be _sooo_
bad, then it is also (by definition) bad enough to warrant banning it.
If it isn't, then the problem isn't big enough to be worth tinkering
with card text to try to tweak it.

DZ
AW

Messages.Author: James Coupe
Messages.Body:
In message <8bCdnfK4c6KGTVTY...@giganews.com>, Derek Ray

<moot@i_dont_check_the_spamtrap_anyway.com> writes:
>James Coupe wrote:
>> In a VC/Awe combo, why is it not Awe that is overpowered?
>
>Awe's cost/effect is actually somewhat balanced. You spend a lot of
>blood off a vampire, you get a lot of votes... once.

In some ways, though, it takes the politics out of politics. Other
similar effects are either played after a successful referendum (e.g.
Cryptic Rider), or are announced in advance (Dia de los Muertos), or are
highly conditional (Malkavian Rider Clause). Though Awe costs a lot of
blood, it just says "Okay, we've negotiated and stuff but, screw you
guys, I'm having my way." Which, at a level of taste and a level of,
erm, what I think the game was supposed to be about, I don't like.
Politics was supposed to be subject to negotiation.

That's a different argument, but it's probably why I come down against
Awe a little more than VC.

>So, avoiding the word "overpowered" since it's subjective and irrelevant
>to the discussion: which card is the strongest in the Awe/VC combo? The
>card that costs lots of blood for lots of votes, or the card that
>removes the cost of the first one, lets you end up with more blood than
>you started with, and gains you 2 pool as well?

Put another way, which is the more powerful - the card that lets you get
your way, or the card that hinges on you already having done so?

>Put another way:
>
>How often do you see Awe played without VC in the deck?
>How often do you see VC played without Awe in the deck?

I've certainly seen one played (in a given turn/action) without the
other, so it's not like players aren't amenable to the possibility.
(Though that's sometimes involved a Giant's Blood in hand or similar,
I'm sure.)

I've also seen, much more rarely, a couple of Awes thrown into decks as
a sort of vote offence or defence, when things are pretty screwy.

Also, though, I don't think that you can use the fact that VC is a
popular include in many decks to categorize it is as the stronger of the
two. I see Deflection in a hell of a lot of Dominate decks before I see
Mind Rape, yet Mind Rape is an incredibly powerful card.

>> I can totally agree that VC/Awe is near the top of the power curve these
>> days. But if it's decided that it's over the top of the power curve, I
>> don't see that it's obvious that it's VC that's the problem. If the
>> reasoning is going:
>>
>> - VC/Awe is overpowered
>> - it would be convenient to nerf VC for reasons of design creativity so
>> we'll nerf that one, even if nerfing Awe would be a better idea
>
>I don't think that's the reasoning at all. I think the reasoning is
>much more like:
>

>-- blood/pool recursion is too prevalent and contributes to game length

>-- VC allows blood/pool recursion for free while still moving forward at
>full speed (KRC, etc.)

>-- VC renders any blood-based costing mechanism for PAs worthless

>-- so, is it possible to nerf VC without hurting big vampires and vote
>decks unnecessarily?

See, if this is the actual reasoning - which it might well be - I think
it's missing a number of important deck types.

Lasombra Breed/Boon, for example, can go forward at full speed, breed at
full speed, and then just tap Power Structure to pass a Con Boon - bing,
6 pool. Bing, another 6 pool. Stealth lets you call the votes, stealth
lets you breed, stealth lets you bleed. Just add Power Structure and a
solid high cap vampire (say, Gratiano) and you're doing very well
indeed. Pretty much zero slowdown on the deck strategy, and lets you
get major, major pool in one action - and it's not entirely incomparable
when you consider that many political decks won't *just* be taking KRC
actions, but also Praxis Seizures, Rumors of Gehenna, or whatever other
support/bolstering votes.

Con Boon has the potential for hugely more pool gain. If pool recursion
is too prevalent *and* is the cause for looking at VC, I think that
looking at Voter Captivation alone is a mis-guided point of change.
Breed/Boon can do frightening things here, and by being a Breed deck is
not sacrificing ousting power in any truly significant way.

--
James Coupe

James Coupe wrote:
> In message <8bCdnfK4c6KGTVTY...@giganews.com>, Derek Ray
> <moot@i_dont_check_the_spamtrap_anyway.com> writes:
>> James Coupe wrote:
>>> In a VC/Awe combo, why is it not Awe that is overpowered?
>> Awe's cost/effect is actually somewhat balanced. You spend a lot of
>> blood off a vampire, you get a lot of votes... once.
>
> In some ways, though, it takes the politics out of politics. Other

So do Delaying Tactics and any number of the anti-vote cards that have
recently been printed that say "No, this vote fails." Not to mention
that there's nothing preventing someone from playing Kindred Coercion on
the vampire who just played Awe.

Awe, played by itself is not an automatic pass for any vote. It is a
powerful tool to help you pass your votes, and it has a
far-from-insignificant cost.

> highly conditional (Malkavian Rider Clause). Though Awe costs a lot of
> blood, it just says "Okay, we've negotiated and stuff but, screw you
> guys, I'm having my way." Which, at a level of taste and a level of,
> erm, what I think the game was supposed to be about, I don't like.
> Politics was supposed to be subject to negotiation.

But there are still plenty of cards available after Awe is played. It's
a strong card with a high cost, but plenty of people in this thread have
already pointed out that no vote is guaranteed to pass, for a number of
reasons that are largely irrelevant to whether Awe was played or not.

Awe doesn't even remotely remove the negotiation from politics...
unless, of course, you figure out a way to play one on every vote. I
wonder how I would go about doing that...

> That's a different argument, but it's probably why I come down against
> Awe a little more than VC.

And at the end, yes, this is a different discussion entirely, about
whether Awe is too big an effect for its cost, and whether Presence
should have such a tool in the first place. Neither is really germane
to the original topic.

>> So, avoiding the word "overpowered" since it's subjective and irrelevant
>> to the discussion: which card is the strongest in the Awe/VC combo? The
>> card that costs lots of blood for lots of votes, or the card that
>> removes the cost of the first one, lets you end up with more blood than
>> you started with, and gains you 2 pool as well?
>
> Put another way, which is the more powerful - the card that lets you get
> your way, or the card that hinges on you already having done so?

A basic tenet of V:TES is "you must be able to build decks that do
things". In other words, take successful actions, call successful
votes, beat people up successfully in combat.

If your vote deck can't pass its votes, Voter Captivation doesn't ever
enter the picture one way or the other. But, in V:TES as in all
well-designed games, offense is stronger than defense and we can safely
assume that in most circumstances, the vote-caller will be able to pass
their vote. Whether they use Awe, or whether they stack a Charming
Lobby and Bewitching Oration on top of some table votes, or _whatever_,
objecting to changes to VC on the grounds of "but it's hard to pass
votes once you get them to referendum and so it's hard to play VC", is,
again, not germane to the discussion. If it was really so hard to pass
votes, vote decks wouldn't be considered a primary archetype.

>> Put another way:
>>
>> How often do you see Awe played without VC in the deck?
>> How often do you see VC played without Awe in the deck?
>
> I've certainly seen one played (in a given turn/action) without the
> other, so it's not like players aren't amenable to the possibility.
> (Though that's sometimes involved a Giant's Blood in hand or similar,
> I'm sure.)

Indeed. I know that in my experience, I _have_ seen one or two Awes
thrown into a PRE deck, alongside a couple "i won't call this vote much,
but it has to pass" votes -- but I have seen Voter Captivation used
routinely in any deck that remotely features superior Presence, whether
it came with Bewitching Oration, Awe, Charming Lobby, Aura of
Invincibility, Legacy of Pander, ... take your pick. There really is no
cost to playing it, as long as you've built a vote deck that expects to
pass most of its votes.

> I've also seen, much more rarely, a couple of Awes thrown into decks as
> a sort of vote offence or defence, when things are pretty screwy.
>
> Also, though, I don't think that you can use the fact that VC is a
> popular include in many decks to categorize it is as the stronger of the
> two. I see Deflection in a hell of a lot of Dominate decks before I see
> Mind Rape, yet Mind Rape is an incredibly powerful card.

Your analogy sort of proves my point -- I consider Deflection to be a
significantly more powerful card than Mind Rape. In fact, it's nearly
on the level of "must have" if your deck features Dominate, unless
you've gone out of your way to avoid needing it.

A card being featured frequently in decks is hardly a sole indicator of
the card's strength. But it is a single valid indicator.

>> I don't think that's the reasoning at all. I think the reasoning is
>> much more like:
>>
>> -- blood/pool recursion is too prevalent and contributes to game length
>> -- VC allows blood/pool recursion for free while still moving forward at
>> full speed (KRC, etc.)
>> -- VC renders any blood-based costing mechanism for PAs worthless
>> -- so, is it possible to nerf VC without hurting big vampires and vote
>> decks unnecessarily?
>
> See, if this is the actual reasoning - which it might well be - I think
> it's missing a number of important deck types.

Whether other forms of bloat should be nerfed isn't yet under
discussion. It may well be a discussion in the future, but the question
wasn't "is bloat too powerful", the question was "should VC be nerfed
and can it be done effectively?"

By the way, I tend to agree that other forms of bloat should come under
discussion too. But for the moment, the topic is VC, and I'm just
pointing out a much more logical reason why VC would be a target for
nerf than "VC decks are too powerful", which is a sky-is-falling
distraction from the original topic.

> Con Boon has the potential for hugely more pool gain. If pool recursion
> is too prevalent *and* is the cause for looking at VC, I think that
> looking at Voter Captivation alone is a mis-guided point of change.

Again, what makes you think anyone is looking at Voter Captivation
alone? That hasn't come up yet, and it's good to remember that just
because a thing hasn't been discussed openly doesn't mean it's not also
under consideration.

For example, nobody has yet considered the possibility of, in the same
set as releasing an MRP to Voter Cap, printing a vote card reading:

Big Momma's Fat Humpin' Orgy
Political Action, 1 blood
Fill a younger vampire that you control to capacity.

Now, this card is far from perfect, I'm sure. But it should illustrate
quite well that nerfing VC might well hardly be the end of the world for
big vampire vote decks... and it should also illustrate that just
because the original question only referred to VC, that it isn't unheard
of that other steps might be taken alongside changing VC.

- --
Derek

Messages.Author: Malone
Messages.Body:
On Feb 7, 12:31 pm, "Robert Goudie" <robe...@vtesinla.org> wrote:

> New Card Text is an inconvenience for existing players but shouldn't
> be an issue for new players. New players are purchasing new cards with
> the new text on them so they're hardly confused.

My experience is that potential new players do not want to begin by
buying new cards. They want to borrow decks to see if they enjoy the
game, then after a while they'll buy a starter deck or two. After
that they mostly rely on free cards that long-time players or ex-
players give them, until they're involved enough to buy a box of
boosters which is often a box of Jyhad because they're still sometimes
really cheap on ebay. And they continue to borrow decks to try out
different clans and strategies. People's experience with the game
suffers a lot from things like "You can't play Majesty, it costs a
blood now" -- one instance of that can ruin a whole game for somebody
(because their empty Anneke was going to survive Tariq's rush with the
Majesty, get hunting ground blood next turn and call Parity Shift
unblockably via TGB... or whatever). And then they may not be back,
because there's a lot of competition for people's gaming time and
money.

Messages.Author: nood...@iprimus.com.au
Messages.Body:
> think that the combo of Awe and Voter
> Cap is an overpowered combination. You don't come to this conclusion by
> *not* playing the combination.

I really don't buy this, sorry. Surely if this combo were overpowered
in an otherwise balanced game, we'd see an overwhelming number of PRE
vote decks winning tournaments. A quick glance at the TWDA will show
that this is simply not the case.

Vote in itself is usually an unwieldy strategy, requiring multiple
cards in particular sequence [vote card, stealth [usually], vote push,
VC] which is quite easily countered by a number of well used cards
[intercept usually, but delaying tactics shows up quite often around
here]. It's a strat that is also boned by happenstance - pred and prey
both pull out fatties [who usually have titles whether you use vote or
not] and every single vote becomes an uphill battle.

Viewed in isolation, card for cost, yes the combo of awe/vc for push,
or the far, far more powerful minion tap/vc for bloat may seem
overpowered. But when viewed in the context of vote decks as an
archetype, and the mechanics of vote in a table situation, it's not at
all overpowered. Vote is a challenging strat to win with, and it's
made competitive by tools like VC.

I say again, if VC were an overpowered card, it would be winning a lot
more tourneys than it does. The proof is in the pudding.

This is not a question of the overpowered nature of VC. I think that's
just misdirection on the part of LSJ. I think this is an issue about
design, and the difficulties LSJ may be facing when exploring the vote
concept in light of VC and cards like KRC and Cons Agg.

Nerfing VC into oblivion [and the suggestions he's made so far are
akin to the 5th Trad nerf, which reduced it to wallpaper] is an easy,
and lazy answer.

thinking.

>
>Note that the ability to get around an obstacle is not the same as
>there being no obstacle.

But there are clear other obstacles in the game that the Design Team has
chosen not to remove.

- It is hard to create an interesting, balanced bleed card for 1 blood,
when Govern the Unaligned is so strong.

- It is hard to create an interesting, balanced bleed card for 0 blood,
when Computer Hacking is very solid indeed.

Yet the Design Team has felt itself able to try out interesting costs
and benefits. See, for example:

- Flurry of Action, free, no bleed, but a nice pay-off
- Enticement, a bleed-like action that isn't a bleed, and so has
interesting pay-offs and benefits, but also restrictions
- Fiendish Tongue, an interesting side benefit (Anarchs) and untap
(Tzimisce) for a sect restriction
- Forgery - an interesting attempt at bleed with a fringe benefit of
bloating

Then Laptop, J.S. Simmons and Tasha Morgan make it hard to create
interesting, generic bleed boosters. But the Design Team has been able
to route around that obstacle and create Robert Carter, with a very
interesting cost.

It is hard to create stealth that's playable without making a given clan
with Dominate over-powered, because of the inherent problems of
Dominate, yet Mirror Walk is a subtle and balanced card dealing with a
pretty significant obstacle.

>All of the designs you imagine the Design Team overlooking are no less
>possible with the obstacle removed than with it in place, and there's
>no indication that they are being overlooked; quite the contrary.

All of the cards that you've created routing around other obstacles have
worked out just fine, even though you could have decided to nerf those
obstacles too.

See also, for example, one of the cards that many people feel is an
inappropriate and huge obstacle to designing for the !Malkavians -
Kindred Spirits. Bleed *and* gain pool at inferior, omni-directable,
and with a bleed bonus at superior! This has generated a LOT of moans
over the years. Yet this obstacle hasn't stopped you creating cards for
the !Malkavians, or bleed modifiers generally, knowing full well they
can be using them.

>Whether the Design Team imagines them is not in question, nor is that
>quesrtion useful toward reaching a conclusion about the question of VC
>being problematic.

It is difficult to see why the Design Team has chosen to focus on Voter
Captivation as an obstacle they must remove, when there are so many
other solid, commonly used, powerful cards that turn up in VAST numbers
of decks using that discipline because they're so very, very good, and
because they're often hugely better cards than other equivalent cards of
the same type for other clans or disciplines.

Somehow, the Design Team seem to have been able to cope with these other
obstacles, and so many more, or make a valiant attempt to do so without
nerfing existing cards.

Why *only* VC? Why have you been able to exercise your creative
imagination(s) to overcome so many other obstacles, but are choosing not
to do so with this one?

I once constructed a highly succesful, tier 1 Ventrue vote deck without a
single Voter Captivation or Parity Shift.

I called it "Kokoomusnuoret" ("The Conservative Youth" or
"Young Republicans").

It had weenie Ventrue and even smaller Caitiff. The Ventrue would play
Revelation of the Sire on the Caitiff, making a swarm of tiny Ventrue.

Then I would slap down Ventrue Directorate Assembly, and go to town with
Praxis Seizures, Con Boons and damaging votes.

I didn't use Voter Captivation, since most of my guys didn't have presence.
Parity Shift would have been counterproductive, since I was planning on
bloating constantly.

One can create a Lasombra deck like this using Power Structure, or !Toreador
with Foundation Exhibit. Most players use Embraces and Creation Rites
instead of Revelation of the Sire.

(RotS had an additional benefit: I could call the vamps in my crypt with the
names of real, living and active young Conservative Finnish politicians. :-)

Messages.Author: Peter D Bakija
Messages.Body:
On Feb 8, 5:09 am, James Coupe <j...@zephyr.org.uk> wrote:

> But there are clear other obstacles in the game that the Design Team has
> chosen not to remove.
>
> - It is hard to create an interesting, balanced bleed card for 1 blood,
> when Govern the Unaligned is so strong.
>
> - It is hard to create an interesting, balanced bleed card for 0 blood,
> when Computer Hacking is very solid indeed.

I don't know that this is the same issue--yeah, Govern is really good
at 1 blood. But since Govern has existed (i.e. forever), plenty of
reasonably good bleed cards built on the same model have been printed
(Scouting Mission--arguably a perfectly good card; Slaughtering the
Herd--arguably not that good as a bleed card, but I'd think more folks
would be looking at this card in the face of the Imbued) and will
continue to be designed and printed. Yeah, ok, none of them are as
*good* as Govern, generally speaking--Scouting should be, but much
like Threats vs Conditioning, the 1 blood cost for 1 extra payload is
a better deal that it costs--but at least they fit into the design
paradigm and are theoretically balanced, and there is nothing built
into the game to specifically counteract the cost.

Like, if there were an action modifier that was "Play during a bleed.
If this bleed is successful, the acting vampire gains blood equal to
the pool lost by the target", A) I think most folks would agree that
it was completely insane and B) it would make cards like Slaughtering
the Herd (arguably not that good as a bleed card, sure, as the one
extra blood cost for the "unblockable by allies" part isn't that much
of an improvement) impossible to design and cost correctly.

Currently, you can't really give a Political Action a blood cost and
expect it to mean anything (unless it is either absurdly huge or you
tack on an arbitrary "you can't gain blood during this vote", which is
both, ya know, kind of arbitrary and likely often *too much* of a cost
for certain effects). It would be perfectly possible to make, say, a
bunch of PAs that were Praxis Seizures or Crusades that each came with
a generic useful special ability (get an extra vote when you call a PA
with the acting Prince, get to untap if you successfully pass a
referendum with the acting Prince, whatever), and give them all an
added cost in blood or pool. But Voter Cap makes this a losing design
situation, as the blood/pool cost is effectively nullified, and then
some. Which is a different issue than trying to make a bleed card that
is equivalent to Govern.

> Then Laptop, J.S. Simmons and Tasha Morgan make it hard to create
> interesting, generic bleed boosters. But the Design Team has been able
> to route around that obstacle and create Robert Carter, with a very
> interesting cost.

Yeah. He costs blood. Funny, that...

> It is difficult to see why the Design Team has chosen to focus on Voter
> Captivation as an obstacle they must remove, when there are so many
> other solid, commonly used, powerful cards that turn up in VAST numbers
> of decks using that discipline because they're so very, very good, and
> because they're often hugely better cards than other equivalent cards of
> the same type for other clans or disciplines.

I think there is a significant difference between the obstacles you
bring up (which are certainly valid examples of design issues that
need dealing with) and the Voter Cap issue--Voter Cap is a completely
concrete, direct obstacle to both:

A) Making political cards cost blood/pool
and
B) Making political cards that give you blood/pool

Both of which are avenues that are seriously underdeveloped in the
arena of political cards (PAs or modifiers or whatever). That Govern
is so good for 1 blood, or that Dementation has Kindred Spirits is a
more abstract obstacle to design, and while it requires the occasional
sidestep to get around, isn't as cut and dry as Voter Cap.

I think, in the end, if Voter Cap does get changed (and I'm still,
ahem, voting for the very simple "Useable on a successful PA: pre:gain
2 blood; PRE: gain 2 pool), I certainly see that various political
decks will take a hit, and will need re-jiggering. But I'd also expect
that various other political upgrades (in the form of new, useful
cards that bolster up these political decks that have taken a hit) and
crazy new angles and cards that were previously deemed unworkable due
to Voter Cap to follow. Like "Big Mama's Honking Orgy" (or
whatever :-)

-Peter

> Voter Captivation is a scaled effect with a greater effect benefited
> by vampires of greater capacity. The game suffers signifigantly from
> an imbalance in power towards many minions being more viable than a
> few minions. More minions means more actions, and more actions means
> more ousting power, and more ousting power results in quicker games.
>
> One of the fundamental problems that the original designers saw in the
> game was that the game took too long to play and was too complicated.
> Quicker games are a result of more minions acting. Things that slow
> games down are intercept, combat and bloating.
>
> So to make games quicker intercept must be toned down, combat must be
> streamlined and bloating must be eliminated.
>
> Perhaps that wasn't what you were asking for?
>

So just for the record, I think that altering Voter Captivation
presents more problems by causing deck designs on the whole to migrate
to smaller and smaller average crypt capacity than it solves by
"spontaneously innovating new cards" with its change.

votes. Likely enough to pass the PA in most games by enough of a
margin. Without spending any blood. If I had a couple blood leftover,

play Voter Cap, and end up with more blood than I started out with.
And some extra pool. And have done whatever horrible thing to my prey
I was doing anway.

Voter Cap, is mostly irelevant. If you gave a PA a cost of 5 blood,

pool that have been developed since the original Jyhad set, and the

(if any) other action modifiers that give you blood or pool during

'cause the design team is like "Huh. That'd be cool. Except that Voter
Cap already exists..."

> the Design Group.

No, but it does limit their ability to apply standard costs to PA
cards. You don't have to believe this. But I'm pretty certian that
LSJ, as the head of the design group, said, more or less, "the
existance of Voter Cap limits my ability to apply standard costs to PA
cards".

-Peter

>
>The metric supplied by looking at similar effects from other cards, obviously.

That shows that a card is better than another. It doesn't show that one
card is broken. For example, let's take a look at some permanent vote
gainers:

- Alamut: slow to gain votes, very hard to use as a shock factor, keys
politics off a second strategy (bleed)
- Oxford University, England: very expensive, only suitable for
extensive use in a few strategies (such as Parity Shift)
- Ventrue Directorate Assembly: expensive, but non-unique. Very
fragile, in most circumstances - the built in action is very
tempting and easy to use, even if you do include a butt-load of
2nd Tradition
- Mausoleum, Venice: vulnerable to being screwed up by another player,
and not a terribly large amount of votes available
- Vox Senis: generates multiple votes, and for every action, but
vulnerable to negotiation since each vote is controlled by a
different Methuselah

Then compare them to Power Structure:

- Power Structure: generates a potentially large number of votes. Not
fragile. Not prone to the whims of other Methuselahs (it's
"every Lasombra you control", not even "every Lasombra").
Doesn't key off a completely different strategy - just bring out
vampires.

Isn't Power Structure a lot better than the other cards, taking its
mechanics in the round? With a naive mechanics comparison, why do we
not decide that Power Structure is broken? Why do we typically decide
that the other cards have issues?

We could do the same with vampire theft cards. Mind Rape and Spirit
Marionette are significantly more pokey than Temptation or Corruption
(from the clan and discipline that's supposed to have been good at
this!).

How are you moving from "(much) better" to "overpowered"? And how are
you accounting for a politics being designed to do some things that
other straegies aren't?

Bleed doesn't have much by way of blood gain, for example, whereas
politics and combat do.

Just looking at mechanics has never been a decisive metric.

>The competitive environment also shows the same: that VC is too
>powerful (by witnessing the effect it has when played in those environs
>-- the same effect it has when played in any other eviron). Just
>because you don't find that the competitive environ shows that it is
>broken doesn't alter that.

Would you care to cite examples of tournaments that show it's
overpowered? Not just very good for its deck, but actually overpowered.

Voter Captivation is far from the only effective method of gaining pool.

(Alternately, if it were, it would then be by definition overpowered;
QED. But it's not, and pretending that it is serves no purpose other
than to distract from the discussion.)

> is limited (combat is promoted as a mechanic), I should surely go mad.

mechanic. No such assumption is warranted. I think we all would prefer
not to see the game turn into Rockem-Sockem-Robots.

suddenly become knee-jerk defensive... especially if the design of the

isn't the correct way to accomplish what needs to be accomplished. But
if people would spend half the time discussing whether it were possible
to change VC effectively that they do screaming that card changes are
bad and "VC isn't broken!!", then perhaps we could have already all
gotten to that point and begun looking in other directions.

>Yeah, ok, none of them are as
>*good* as Govern, generally speaking--Scouting should be, but much
>like Threats vs Conditioning, the 1 blood cost for 1 extra payload is
>a better deal that it costs--but at least they fit into the design
>paradigm and are theoretically balanced, and there is nothing built
>into the game to specifically counteract the cost.

This isn't just a Dominate thing, though. Computer Hacking makes it
very difficult to create a neat card for a particular discipline (or
title, trait, or whatever) that is just +1 bleed - why not play Computer
Hacking? If Computer Hacking had been weaker - perhaps, 1 blood, Do Not
Replace - it would be much easier to design in that gap.

Yet the Design Team have happily explored alternatives costs,
punishments and benefits for bleeds and bleed-like actions, without
feeling the need to nerf cards that are design obstacles. Remember:

All of the designs you imagine the Design Team overlooking are
no less possible with the obstacle removed than with it in
place,

But the very common "power cards" are and have been design obstacles to
creating new, vibrant cards for other disciplines. Yet the Design Team
have chosen to work around the obstacles.

>Like, if there were an action modifier that was "Play during a bleed.
>If this bleed is successful, the acting vampire gains blood equal to
>the pool lost by the target", A) I think most folks would agree that
>it was completely insane and B) it would make cards like Slaughtering
>the Herd (arguably not that good as a bleed card, sure, as the one
>extra blood cost for the "unblockable by allies" part isn't that much
>of an improvement) impossible to design and cost correctly.

Probably so, but this is something that a naive mechanic comparison
won't reveal. Oh look, Hypothetical Bleed Mod is about the same as VC,
re-fill a vampire for doing what it does.

But that's why naive mechanics comparisons are, frankly, a complete
crock of shit.

Where to start:

1) It is massively easier to bleed for a lot than it is to vote for a
lot. You bleed for 8 and get 8 blood. I vote to do you 3
damage (KRC) and get 8 blood from a Voter Cap. Difference =
large. I *cannot* increase the amount of damage a KRC does.

2) A bleed is blocked by one Methuselah. A vote is always blocked by
two, until the end game. Your combat wall predator gets a
chance to block the vote called by a mostly empty Arika, but not
the chance to block the bleed.

3) Bleeds are not subject to referenda. You get enough stealth and
don't get bounced, you win. It is not subject to Methuselahs
voting it down, and bounce can be compared in many ways to
Delaying Tactics or Vox Domini.

4) To play VC, the vote must be successful. That is, I set the terms,
and those terms must have been enforced by a successful
referenda. Not true with your bleed modifier, in that it can
still be played on a bounce, and will benefit from the bounce.
Were it "Only usable when you successfully bleed your prey", you
might be doing something better.

5) Bleding is the most efficient ousting mechanism in the game. Having
a powerful blood gain mechanism available to the most efficient
ousting mechanism in the game seems less useful. That politics
is less efficient as an ousting mechanism, by apparently
conscious design choice, means that you can very probably give
it nicer toys.

>Currently, you can't really give a Political Action a blood cost and
>expect it to mean anything (unless it is either absurdly huge or you
>tack on an arbitrary "you can't gain blood during this vote", which is
>both, ya know, kind of arbitrary and likely often *too much* of a cost
>for certain effects). It would be perfectly possible to make, say, a
>bunch of PAs that were Praxis Seizures or Crusades that each came with
>a generic useful special ability (get an extra vote when you call a PA
>with the acting Prince, get to untap if you successfully pass a
>referendum with the acting Prince, whatever), and give them all an
>added cost in blood or pool. But Voter Cap makes this a losing design
>situation, as the blood/pool cost is effectively nullified, and then
>some. Which is a different issue than trying to make a bleed card that
>is equivalent to Govern.

It certainly means *something*. How many VCs do you pack in the deck?
A browse through the TWDA recently showed up 6-8 copies in a lot of
situations, which seems perfectly adequate for most purposes. You won't
always have one in hand, and if you have other votes to call, you won't
always have the right vote or the right vampire to call it.

If the vote itself is more controversial, more indiscriminate, or more
likely to invoke the ire of other Methuselahs, you may well find
yourself unable to pass it by a large amount. (Oh, except for Awe...)
See, for example, Trumped-Up Charges as one political action where other
Methuselahs are given votes to thwart you.

>> Then Laptop, J.S. Simmons and Tasha Morgan make it hard to create
>> interesting, generic bleed boosters. But the Design Team has been able
>> to route around that obstacle and create Robert Carter, with a very
>> interesting cost.
>
>Yeah. He costs blood. Funny, that...

A nicely glib response, but missing the point. He costs blood. 1
blood. Woo.

Now look at the *rest* of the card. He has an upkeep cost. If you
don't *keep* paying blood, you lose the effect. If someone comes and
pounds you in combat, you may well find yourself empty at the start of
your turn and so lose the card.

That is more than *just* VC can cope with. You need to keep blood on
you at all times, or lose the card. Could you do something similar with
a vote card? You bet your ass you could.

And before we get all "Oh, but Robert Carter decks won't be able to
regain blood *at all* like the VC decks will", let's remember that there
are plenty of ways of gaining blood, if you choose to design for it.
Fifth gives a nice hunk of blood, so does Renewed Vigor. Jake
Washington can give you 4 whole blood. Entrenching can give you a lot
of blood on a big vampire. Harvest Rites and the Hungry Coyote can give
the Sabbat a very potent blood gain package. And you can do all this
with a weenie and Heidelberg it over.

>Both of which are avenues that are seriously underdeveloped in the
>arena of political cards (PAs or modifiers or whatever). That Govern
>is so good for 1 blood, or that Dementation has Kindred Spirits is a
>more abstract obstacle to design, and while it requires the occasional
>sidestep to get around, isn't as cut and dry as Voter Cap.

So the Design Team can design around other obstacles that are abstract,
but can't design around one that is obvious and in front of it. Even
when this thread has included a *massive* amount of suggestions of how
to do exactly that.

Look at how many votes LSJ has designed that require a Prince or
Justicar, which has apparently been a perfectly reasonable cost for,
say, Parity Shift or First Tradition. When strong cards like those can
be balanced with a specific sect and title requirement, do we need to go
into blood or pool costs?

And why do we need to go into blood and pool costs at all, when so many
other costing mechanisms are available? Just because blood and pool are
simple?

That seems, you know, dumb.

That is the crux of a great deal of this discussion. How much does a
cost mean when it is incredibly easy to counteract that cost. For my
money, the answer is "not that much". I could bring up every
convoluted example in the world about how a blood cost of 1 or a
combat card is much more significant than a blood cost of 1 for a
political card, but those examples have already been made. A bunch of
times. So I'll skip that part. But in the end, simply from the
experience of playing a lot, personally, I never find the blood costs
associated with vote cards (and vote strategies) to be remotely an
issue in decks that use Voter Cap; playing Awe, Eldar Impersonation,
Forgotten Labyrinth, whatever, simply don't have the same impact in a
Presence based vote deck than they do in non Voter Cap enabled decks.
Sure, of course there is *some* cost (i.e. paying a blood when you
play a vote card means you have one less blood for Awe; paying a pool
for a vote card means you only gain one pool off the voter Cap), but
the issue is "how significant is that cost". And again, for my money,
Voter Cap makes costs like this mostly insignificant.

> A nicely glib response, but missing the point. He costs blood. 1
> blood. Woo.

Heh. I thought so too :-)

In any case, my point (in response to your point, which is like having
a point in every direction, which is like having no point at all...)
is that Rober Carter costs blood. Not just the blood to recruit him,
but the blood to upkeep him. Which is slightly different than him just
costing X blood to start with. But not that much, and still, is
relying on the "simple" costing mechanism--he costs blood. Which is
the simple costing mechanism that the deisgn team seems to feel is
compromised for use on political cards. Even if it is a "1 blood per
turn" cost, instead of just a "pay X blood now" cost. If Robert Carter
had a non simple cost (i.e. that cost something *other* than blood),
such as "Discard a card that requires a discipline during your untap,
or burn Robert Carter" or "While Robert Carter is in play, you get 4
fewer transfers", then he'd be a good example of a "creative" costing
mechanism (like, say, Fiendish Tongue compared to Computer Hacking).

> So the Design Team can design around other obstacles that are abstract,
> but can't design around one that is obvious and in front of it. Even
> when this thread has included a *massive* amount of suggestions of how
> to do exactly that.

Sure--they obviously *can* do so (see: Eldest Command Undeath). But it
seems like a problem that they feel (presumably) that the "simple"
costing mechanism is out of their reach. And as the single card that
puts it out of their reach is likely too powerful anyway, the math
does itself.

> That seems, you know, dumb.

Well, ya know, I don't think so. But that is me.

This is true, but due to the way Vote decks work, it is easier to pass
a vote than it is to stop a vote, due to cards like Bewitching and
Awe. Having two vote decks sitting next to each other is a very
different situation than having two combat decks sitting next to each
other--two combat decks adjacent end up with both of them getting
killed. Two vote decks next to each other tend to result in a fairly
normal relationship, and the one who draws more vote push tends to
come out on top. I don't know about you, but when I see Vote decks at
the table (or play vote decks), they tend to successfully pass votes a
lot more often than not. Even if there are other Vote decks at the
table.

> nothing more than a statistical anomaly that will be erased if voter
> captivation is weakened

I don't think this is actually true. Vote decks are pretty successful
across the board. They are certainly more successful at ousting folks
than Combat decks are.

-Peter

> Indeed, that was the primary reason for the request for comments in my initial

The problem there is that you've made your determination of VC based
on the subjective metric of your personal judgement. The most
objective argument I can make is one of game balance, which you're
dismissing because it determines "brokenness" and not
"overpoweredness". I'm then left to using the same metric that you're
using - subjective judgement.

At which point, the argument devolves to my opinion versus your
opinion. As much as I like my own opinion, I don't like the use of
mere opinion comparisons for making a decision on this. Perhaps
you'll grant weight to the collective opinion regarding the matter
here on the newsgroup (insert jokes here), but even then, it wouldn't
be a matter of reasoned argument (insert more jokes here), but one of
an opinion poll.

If I seem exasperated with you about this (ok, I am), it's because
I'm used to arguing with you in objective terms, not subjective terms.

For what they may be worth, here are my opinions on the matter:

As far as I can tell, blood costs are irrelevant to the costing of
political action cards (Eldest Command Undeath excepted), as the
requirements and overhead for playing a political game are high
enough. As it stands, PTO is the only political action with a blood
cost, and one is certainly not going to be fretting about getting that
one blood back. There are other political actions for which I would
be more than happy to pay a blood for: Ancient Influence, Political
Stranglehold, Con Boon, Reins of Power, Parity Shift, Banishment,
Brinksmanship (already costs a pool), Archon, Alastor, and maybe even
KRC, just off the top of my head. Compared to the vampires I have to
bring out, the vote lock I have to get, and everything else that goes
with getting a political deck to succeed, the cost of a blood seems
irrelevant to me. Certainly the cost gets more and more relevant the
higher the blood cost gets, but as it stands, I'm perfectly content
with the costing scheme of requirements and overhead for political
actions. I don't see what blood costs for political actions would
really add to the game, apart from having more special cases like
Eldest Command Undeath - and if they're special cases, then doing the
textual dance around VC seems fine.

With regards to requirements and overhead for political actions, I
feel that you haven't done enough in that area in your development of
the game. To date, you've made only two political actions with a clan
requirement (Heirophant and Dogs of War), and I feel that this avenue
should be explored. To date, you've made only one political action
that requires a Justicar or Inner Circle Member (Alastor), and none
that require a Prince or Primogen. Again, I feel that this avenue
should be explored. I would also like to see more clan-based
political action modifiers and reactions, as a way to represent a
clan's ability to affect the political sphere in ways that their
disciplines cannot.

When it comes to issues of design hindrance, I find it intriguing
that you're focussing on Voter Captivation, when Parity Shift and PTO
appear to me to be more of a design hindrance. You may feel that VC
is freebie bloat, but isn't Parity Shift even more so since the pool
loss (what you were doing anyway) and the bloat are contained in one
card? Isn't it difficult to design a political action for Justicars
and Inner Circle Members since you have to come up with something that
is good enough to play with alongside of or instead of PTO? Perhaps
it is coincidence that you haven't created political actions for
Princes and only one for Justicars and IC Members, but it doesn't look
that way to me.

I know you're not keen on bringing "brokenness" into this
discussion, but it seems to me that if a given card appears to be
overpowered, yet not disruptive to the game balance or gameplay, then
other, similar cards might need to be brought to the level of the card
you're worried about, rather than bringing that card down. Certainly
one can't balance a game by making everything equally unbalanced, but
perhaps it is the weaker cards that are out of balance.

I really don't want 12 years' worth of Voter Captivations with
incorrect text. I know that there are already 200+ cards with changed
text, and adding one more might not seem like a big deal, but we have
to draw the line somewhere or else the game's integrity suffers more
than it already does. Please save text changes for matters of
mechanical necessity.

I understand and can clearly see that the original Jyhad set has
numerous legacy problems with respect to future design. In an ideal
world, you could just throw out that set and start again, but that
would obviously be too disruptive. However, it appears that what
you're doing is very slowly and gradually reworking that set, combined
with making new cards that help steer the direction of the game to
where it "should" be. While I've agreed with nearly all of the
changes you've made to the original Jyhad cards, I think you can stop
reworking that set now.

- Ben Peal

What you're trying to say is "Just because something uses politics
doesn't mean it can't be broken."

Well, duh.

None of the people participating in the discussion are five years old
and unable to cope with this truly radical concept.

> Everything that you are saying about vote
>cards as an example of what is not so good about Voter Cap is as true
>for the worst vote card (Regaining the upper Hand?) as it is of the best
>vote card (Parity Shift?) According the the logic of "but voting is
>hard", there is no valid way to say that Parity Shift is good while
>Regaining the Upper Hand is bad.

That's just crap.

The logic of "voting is hard" is just that - voting is hard. It is
simply not as easy as bleed. Thus, wild comparisons of "Hey, this card
would be totally broken if we gave it to bleed" are, perhaps,
interesting but ultimately don't mean a whole lot. Nor does creating a
broken vote card.

They show that politics can be broken, not that Voter Captivation is
broken.

And there are plenty of valid ways of showing that Parity Shift is good
while Regaining the Upper Hand isn't (save for some corner case Form of
Corruption type situations, where it is still difficult).

You could start with a naive mechanics comparison, and here that would
have some validity, because they're both votes. We're not comparing
Renewed Vigor with Awe, we're comparing a vote with a vote. And the
naive mechanics comparison would show the possibility of a 10 pool swing
(5 down, 5 up) or some combination spread among multiple Methuselahs,
relative to gaining the Edge. Then the concept of gaining and losing
pool as a strategy to winning would probably win out against Regaining
the Upper Hand.

Then we could start on evidence of tournaments and competitive play
generally (i.e. anything other than a demo for noobs, or pissing around
in a casual game with fun decks, or some really whacked out Build Your
Own Storyline where the usual assumptions don't hold). We could see
that, in practise, the decks using Parity Shift do better than the decks
using Regaining the Upper Hand. And we could see the swing that Parity
Shift brings about when played - taking you from a (usually intentional)
weaker position to a stronger position, and such.

One example of this would be found in the Tournament Winning Deck
Archive. Parity Shift turns up many times, in many political decks with
Princes or Justicars on hand. Regaining the Upper Hand, first printed
in the same set as Parity Shift, turns up... zero times.

But what you can't do is just say "Well, it would be totally broken if a
bleed could take 5 pool from a Methuselah and give me that 5 pool!" and
expect that to stand up to rigorous scrutiny, just like you can't say
"Well, it would be totally broken if bleed got Voter Captivation!" and
expect that to prove that Voter Captivation is overpowered.

Other things that bleed can't do include:

- giving you and your friends extra master phase actions
- burning vampires of your choice (Eldest Command Undeath, Protect Thine
Own)
- prevent people from taking a turn without paying a stiff price.

And few people would want bleed to be able to do these things. But
similarly, we wouldn't say "Man, it would be totally broken if you gave
these things to bleed, so they're broken for vote."

And why does politics get to do things like this? One facet is
because... voting is hard. Another facet is that... the direct ousting
element of voting is generally less efficient than bleed.

You cannot evaluate Voter Captivation in isolation, saying "Well, that
applies to all votes." That's pretty much the entire point. It applies
to all votes. Voter Captivation is inextricably linked with votes. You
cannot separate Voter Captivation from the need to be successful at
politics. Fifth Tradition is just an action. Renewed Vigor is just an
action. Bleed + Hypothetical VC-like Mod is a bleed action. And since
bleeds are easier and more efficient than votes, the fringe benefits
should - in general - be generally weaker.

>'Cause voting is hard. So no vote will
>ever get called or passed. So that Parity shift is good and Regaining
>the Upper Hand is bad is irrelevant. 'Cause in the world of "but voting
>is hard", neither of them will ever be successfully called anyway.

No, they can both be called, and both be passed. But it's harder. It
needs more setup. It's vulnerable at more points.

Solid bleed requires a 3 cap with Obf + Bleed discipline (Presence,
Dominate, Dementation being obvious candidates). Solid vote requires
more effort - vampires with titles, setup actions with Praxis Seizures
(that need to pass), permanent vote gain masters (that you need to put
in play).

This isn't "Oh woe is politics, it can't do anything." It's
acknowledging that politics isn't the same as other strategies, and has
a number of weaknesses compared to other strategies - and so has been
granted various bonuses compared to other strategies.

>> I don't see it around here, because titled vampires are common and
>> people hate votes on the face of them. Combat and Intercept is
>> popular as well.
>
>You don't see vote decks work? Ever? I don't know what to tell you. 6 of
>the 20 most recent TWDs are heavily vote related. So apparently, they
>can win.

They can, and I doubt he's saying they can't. It's just that people do
play vote defence, and so it's not a no-brainer by any stretch, and
suffers from all sorts of likely problems which slow it down, and mean
that Voter Captivation isn't played on every vote to generate TWENTY
SEVEN BILLION POOL.

Apparently, no-one round you has discovered vote defence. But that's
like saying we should downgrade bleed because no-one plays Deflection,
even though when defended against well, bleed has its own problems (and
compensatory benefits - like, you know, winning).

requires a bare minimum of two cards but realistically more like four
or five. I know you know this, and I know it's been said repeatedly
in this thread, so why do you keep making the inapt analogies?

Does Voter Captivation give an excessive reward for the effort
involved, and is it so excessive that it's worth changing or banning,
that's the point. You have said explicitly that you believe so, and
the 'voting is hard' people are saying that they believe not in a way
that's clear enough that I don't see why you insist on reading it as
meaning that they think *no* reward would be too big for a successful
politician.

I personally think the VC reward is slightly excessive (and that there
are many, many other cards with slightly excessive rewards), and that
the excess does not merit the extreme interventions proposed. It's
one of the big cards in the game, and one of very few associated with
voting. If it's keeping voting from getting new big cards, well,
that's not a disaster. There's no reason at all it should keep voting
from getting new interesting, useable cards.

Referrendums fail a lot around here. Two or more political decks at
the table is not uncommon. I personally do put one or two Delaying
Tactics and a Poison Pill in just about every deck that doesn't have
some other defense against politics. I see DT in other people's decks
occasionally too, and there's a fair amount of Scalpel Tongue around.

That would be because the post was disputing Peter's points, which seem
to largely be:

1) But it would be so broken if we gave it to bleed.

which is an invalid point, because vote isn't bleed.

2) Here's some made up vote card that's broken. Now *that* proves that
VC is broken, doesn't it?

which is similarly wrong.

Since I wasn't making a pro-VC post, but rather disputing Peter's
methods, it's not surprising that something that wasn't in the post,
erm, wasn't in the post.

>I fully agree with you on politics ...(requote)
>> This isn't "Oh woe is politics, it can't do anything." It's
>> acknowledging that politics isn't the same as other strategies, and has
>> a number of weaknesses compared to other strategies - and so has been
>> granted various bonuses compared to other strategies.
>
>but the bonuses should be limited to political actions. some
>referendums (referenda?) are stronger in result than what you can have
>outside politics, fine.

The bonuses from Voter Captivation are only available on political
actions.

Note also that many other strategies have cards that are not part of the
strategy itself but which give you a bonus when utilizing the strategy
well.

For example, if vampires calling votes and then gaining blood when they
pass is off-limits, ban Guru - and potentially Perfectionist. Note that
Perfectionist applies to many, many strategies in the game.

Similarly, combat should only benefit from the combat, so let's remove
Fame, Tension in the Ranks, Provisions of the Silsila, Soul Stealing,
Predator's Transformation...

Bleed must have Capitalist banned, and Alamut is clearly right out.

>Why do i have to add to this a card that modifies the referendum in
>such a good way that i would never think to play a political deck
>without?

Several problems with this:

1) There are numerous political decks that are played without Voter
Captivation. Most of them don't involve Presence. For example,
Auspex-based cancellation, found with the !Ventrue, can do
really very well. Nosferatu Royalty can do well without going
near Presence - though one or two do have Presence if you choose
to go that way, but one of those is Harrod, which is awkward, as
the Inner Circle title is a pain (for once!) because you can't
Parity Shift or Second Tradition. Big Gangrel decks can do very
well using (for example) Ingrid and Stanislava, with no Voter
Captivation or Awe on hand. A number of less subtle combat
decks can vote by rushing troublesome vampires (e.g. burning
Arika) and calling the more controversial votes afterwards. The
Lasombra have access to Power Structure, and can vote pretty
well with that. The EuroBrujah have very little access to
Presence (CEL/POT/DOM on Donal and Constanza, CEL/pot on
Volker), and can still put together a reasonable voting package
through pool gain and titles.

2) There are numerous cards that are found in similar fashions. So many
decks involving combat play Taste of Vitae, for example. Why do
I need to add this card that modifies the combat in such a good
way? It's hard to imagine playing a deck with a reasonable
number of Dominate vampires that *doesn't* play Deflection.

2a) Perhaps the best example of a card that almost must be played when
it is available is Freak Drive. If you're playing big vampires
with Fortitude, you almost have to include Freak Drive. You get
the flexibility of Forced March instead these days, but Freak
Drive is a stunning, stunning card. It's also the case that
when people evaluate new vampires, any big vampire without
reliable access to untap tech (particularly Freak Drive) get a
number of negative remarks, unless there's something specific
about them that negates that. The huge significance of cards
like that makes Voter Captivation pale, IMO.

>I personally don't like cards that SHOULD go in every deck of a type
>and VC is THE card in presence vote decks (that is, by strong majority
>i imagine, vote decks)

Big vampire decks have long had the problem of almost needing to use
Minion Tap. Aside from ally heavy decks (specifically, the Imbued)
practically every strong deck in the game uses either Minion Tap or
Blood Doll, with occasional side helpings of Tribute to the Master
(though its indiscriminate nature means it isn't always well liked).

Deflection goes into vast, vast numbers of Dominate decks. Heart of
Nizchetus looks like it may end up being found in vast numbers of decks.
Auspex decks not using the Bowl of Convergence usually should think
again. Vast numbers of decks use one of the (now) three available Wake
cards.

This isn't a new thing.

>As an example I think that having votercap as a political action would
>be seen as a perfectly viable PA, fits in some decks, not in others,
>would not be played in all presence political deck but is useful for
>bloat in a non vote heavy environment.

As I've said elsewhere in this thread, it's probably the case that Voter
Captivation was written in an overly broad fashion. It would be,
perhaps, nice if Voter Captivation's effect required something else in
addition, so that alternative Voter Cap-like effects could be created
for other situations.

But we've had cards like this before, where the majority (perhaps the
overwhelming majority) of decks capable of playing the card choose to
play the card, and we still have such cards in the game without touching
them.

There is a difference between a card being appropriate for many kinds of
deck and a card being overly powerful. The former creates design
problems (such as, how to design new cards, or how to design "clones"
that are worth playing for other disciplines/sects/traits, how to
diversify deck designs), but design problems are not the same as power
problems.

>> Second Tradition's text change resolved a common problem with it, htat

>It was also given a blood cost for the untap, which wasn't strictly

Actually, again, this wasn't a straight-forward nerf. The V:TES text,
from the WotC card text files:

Card Text: Requires ready Prince or Justicar.
Only usable by a tapped vampire. Untap this
vampire. This reacting vampire gets +2 intercept.

The card had moved from "Usable by a tapped vampire" in Jyhad to "Only
usable" in V:TES. The rewrite by LSJ makes it better again (usable by
tapped and untapped), resolves the issue of zero-stealth actions for
tapped vampires (which a straight-forward application of the rules
denied), and gives it a minor cost for tapped vampires. So it's up AND
down. Which isn't an outright nerf.

>> Drawing Out The Beast and Weather
>> Control could both shut down any vampire, by virtue of being stackable
>> and, in the case of DotB, taking effect at the end of the round (so S:CE
>> couldn't save you).
>
>Fair enough. DotB and WC probably were "broken" in the sense that they
>*needed* fixing. But Second Traditon?

I think you're forgetting what the change to Second Tradition actually
was, in favour of a rose-tinted version in which LSJ only nerfed the
card. He didn't.

>And even 5th Tradition was
>arguably just "really really good" rather than "broken".

Arguably, evidence from actual play contradicted this. As others have
pointed out, Fifth Tradition almost formed its own strategy - Fifth,
Minion Tap, push out some more vampires with your Info Highways (or
whatever).

That's very different to the card under consideration, where you need to
be successful in a strategy that's central to the game to use it - one
of the three strategies Garfield set up. If being successful at votes
is too easy (for whatever reason), then we should look at why - is it a
degenerate case of a group that's only playing pro-vote, or is it more
of a case (taken in the round) of the available cards being unsuitable,
or is it the case that some strategies/clans being denied useful access
to cards that are suitable for others? Or whatever.

> And
>Banishment wasn't "broken" when you could banish anyone--just really,
>really good.

1 caps banishing 11 caps (as did happen) was generally considered to be
beyond "really, really good." But this wasn't established just by
looking at card text, but also by virtue of seeing the effect of the
card in play.

It is possible - though by no means certain - that this was focused on
because of the strength of Legacy of Pander (which was nerfed in SW,
Banishment in FN). We had similar nerfs going before that, though, with
the aggravated damage rules being rolled back from the power in V:TES to
something closer to the power in Jyhad (but somewhat simpler), *and* a
fix for Pulled Fangs (which was still considered too powerful even with
that fix to aggravated damage).

> And did Delaying Tactics *need* to cost a blood? Was the
>game being shut down by free Delaying Tactics? Unlikely--it was just
>likely too powerful for a disciplineless card and could use a nerfing.

This is perhaps the most obvious "power card" that wasn't exactly
broken. But a one blood cost to it doesn't completely rewrite a whole
strategy in the way that completely altering how Voter Cap would to (a
lot of) Presence voters. It just makes it a slightly less no-brain
defence.
