Messages.Author: Joshua Duffin
Messages.Body:
"LSJ" <vte...@white-wolf.com> wrote in message
news:x%1xh.6667$zH1....@newssvr29.news.prodigy.net...

> Anyway, Voter Cap seems to be an obstacle to making any balanced PA cards
> with costs. The few I've attempted have been backed into the corner of
> textual acrobatics like Eldest Command Undeath. Even that is suspect due
> to the option of alternating referendums between the costly-ones and the
> Voter Capped ones.

Hmm. To briefly address the design aspect of the question, I think textual
acrobatics like Eldest Command Undeath are a very appropriate solution to
that issue. Other variants, like "cannot gain more than 1 blood during this
action" or "cannot play action modifiers during this action" would give
interesting design options as well. Then, too, there are many possible
"requires X" options for political-action design (requires a titled
independent vampire; requires a Giovanni; requires a Sabbat vampire;
requires a vampire of capacity above 5; etc etc), and historically those
appeared to be considered as the appropriate "costs" for political action
cards - there were no political actions that cost blood in Jyhad, and up
through Sabbat, only Protect Thine Own had any printed cost at all.

> Voter Cap itself may be the problem.
>
> It is the only card that grants such easy blood gain (repeatable,
> unblockable, restrictions amounting only to: if your deck is working in
> its primary goal in the first place). And then it compounds the effect
> with pool gain to boot.

Just as an aside, "unblockable" is a bit hyperbolic in referring to an
action-modifier card. It's inherent in the nature of action modifiers that
they cannot be blocked, much as it is inherent in the nature of master cards
that they cannot be blocked either.

> Other comparable effects:
> Taste of Vitae: successful combat damage. No pool.
> Giant's Blood: MPA, once per game, no pool gain.
> Fifth Tradition: P/J, action, 1 blood cost, only 4 blood gained, no pool.
> Entrenching: action, 4 blood already, only 4 blood gained, no pool.
> Concert Tour: DoC (not many big-cap DoC), action, 1 blood, delay, no pool.
>
> The closest seems to be Taste of Vitae, which is a pretty powerful card, I
> think we all agree.

Pretty powerful, maybe, but I have not heard of reasonable people suggesting
that it's so strong that it ought to be weakened because it's making the
cost of combat cards insignificant.

> It also gives blood for nothing more than "what you were doing anyhow". It
> is slightly more cyclable (can be played even when damage is prevented or
> not done at all or whatever), but it never gives pool, and it's harder to
> get the same range of gain with damage compared to vote margins, and vote
> margins don't incur the same risks as combat (and, arguably, "doing what
> your deck does" is typically stronger in the "oust your prey" category for
> vote decks than for combat decks).
>
> Thoughts?

Taste of Vitae is disciplineless and Voter Captivation requires Presence -
superior Presence for the pool-gain portion, which appears to be heavily on
your mind, based on the comparisons you made above. That is not an
insignificant cost. Kindred Spirits also gives you pool for what you were
doing anyway, is even more directly tied to ousting your prey than passing
votes is, and is the most cyclable of all (playable whenever you have it in
hand).

The Presence requirement on Voter Captivation - and the requirement for
having enough capacity on the vampire playing Voter Captivation to gain a
substantial benefit from it - appear to be conditions that deserve further
consideration. One, an awful lot of the vote decks that get played in the
first place use Presence, not just for Voter Captivation, but also because
Bewitching Oration, Awe, Charming Lobby, and so on are in the same
discipline. Two, those Presence vote decks don't have easy access to
stealth - a major balancing factor for powerful actions and action-modifiers
like Voter Captivation - unless they are the Setites, who lack powerful
titles and only have titles at all on rather high-capacity vampires. Three,
you can't gain very much blood from a Voter Captivation unless the vampire
you play it with has a large capacity to hold all that blood. High-capacity
vampires are well-known to be less efficient than low-capacity vampires in
general, so it requires using otherwise-less-optimal tools to maximize one's
use of Voter Captivation. Four, requiring a Discipline rather than being a
Disciplineless card justifies, in many many cases, large increases in power
level of the cards in question - from weakish cards like Entrenching to
strong ones like Scouting Mission and Enchant Kindred; from weak cards like
Tortured Confessions to strong ones like Decapitate; from weak cards like
Banner of Neutrality to strong ones like Redirection.

Or, to compare strength to strength, there are other strong cards that
reward you for "what you're doing anyway": Social Charm and Legal
Manipulations for pool while also increasing a bleed and helping oust your
prey; Parity Shift for pool while also reducing your prey's pool; Kindred
Spirits, as mentioned above, for pool while, again, increasing bleeds to
help oust your prey (or someone else if you prefer).

At this point, the hypothesis that Voter Captivation is stronger than it
should be does not appear very well supported by the evidence at hand. More
evidence that it is, in fact, too strong should be presented before taking
action to reduce its strength.

Josh

Messages.Author: Darby Keeney
Messages.Body:
"LSJ" <vte...@white-wolf.com> wrote in message

news:hH%zh.43649$Gr2....@newssvr21.news.prodigy.net...

> Matthew T. Morgan wrote:
>> Small vampires are stronger than they should be. I've never heard anyone
>> refute that statement. Can we get a fix please?
>

> What fix do you propose?

Scott,

First, thanks again for the attention you're giving the topic and the
openness to considering options/opinions before making changes. Second,
this should likely spawn a new thread, but I'll respond here for now.

Some things have already been done within the existing rule set. It seems
appropriate to recognize that progress and then see where one could build
further.

1) The discipline-point equation for larger vampires has been adjusted
upward - giving them more discipline-based card options and flexibility.

2) It appears that there has even been some attempt to create an "in-clan
sub-discipline" which is primarily available in the larger vampires of that
clan. 30% of G3-4 !Nos have [for] and 25% of the G3-4 Tremere have [nec].
When the density of these fourth disciplines is high enough, the larger
vampires can actually begin to consider additional library options.

3) Large vampires have more useful special abilities. Auto-recurrance,
innate rushes vampires, inherent stealth, hand size increase, cost
reduction, vote doubling, etc. are all very good, assuming one actually
builds around the ability and looks beyond vampires as a sack-o-disciplines.

4) There are more cards only useable by in contact with smaller vampires.

I believe that the two area which offers the most promise are:

the 2nd - giving large vampires in a clan connective "out-of-clan"
disciplines

and

the 4th - providing additional "fattie" cards, both inside disciplines
(e.g., Croc Tongue) and outside (e.g., Minor Irritation). I could envision
an expansion which solely focuses as cards only useable by vampires of X
capacity, or by older vampires interacting with younger vampires. It might
go a long way towards advancing the cause of the elder......

Solutions that dramatically alter the rules structure are less favorable
options, in my opinion. We enjoy the game as it is currently designed - to
make wholesale changes might be better considered in a new game. And while
White Wolf did re-design the World of Darkness, I really don't wish to
obsolete my entire card collection in a similar move.

1) A long time ago, the LA group kicked around "Larger vampires an inherent
+1 or +2 bleed, based on capacity" - but I find that a bit problematic,
especially given the impact that "IC +2 bleed" has (especially in concert
with +bleed disciplines).

2) Additional/unlimited influence - I didn't find the unlimited influence
variant we played in Atlanta particularly rewarding - though I will admit
that is mostly due to my deck design philosophy which usually stresses the
building phase of the game.

Cheers.
D.

Oh Noes! David, you're making him think those cards are good enough to
solve the problem! :-) While cards like that are cute and nice and all,
they don't come very close to actually redressing the inherent efficiency
advantages of smaller vampires.

This is IMO because the advantages of smaller vampires are inherent in the
game's mechanics (they cost less pool and have, consequentially, more
actions-per-pool-invested, more blocks-per-pool-invested, and so on).
Printing cards that help bigger vampires means you have to build your deck
with, draw, and play the cards at the right times to gain whatever benefits
they can provide. The smaller vampires have no such requirement to use
their comparative advantages.

I think rules-based fixes would be far more effective than any "cards that
help large vampires more than small ones" you'd be willing to print, Scott.
(Something like "stackable non-unique Aranthebes" might get the job done,
but it might be too large a hammer for your taste in hitting this particular
nail. :-)

Influence changes might do something, sure, but I think the action
advantages over time are the bigger issue. Reducing small vampires'
inherent bleed, votes, strength (or increasing the same for larger vampires,
if you prefer) would be more apropos, I think.

Josh

honestly, yes.

That is: one turn, smart play, marginally competent deck-building skills.
See, granting the weenie predator 14 transfers means the prey (who went first)
gets 11 transfers (one vampire, say a 9, 10, or 11 cap) first turn and then four
transfers second turn (plus any "oh, I've got big cap crypt, so I might need

deck-building) and you've handled a minimum of two, but probably three, maybe
four. Next turn, four more transfers (barring something in your library to speed
that along) and you have your second vampire (11 and 8, or 9 and 10). And so on.

i think adjusting those sorts of things would be very scary from a
play-balance point of view, and playtesting, etc. Also, it'd be complete
structural reform, which tends not to go down very well with the player
base.

I'd, personally, rather see _limits_ in place based on capacity. eg:

a vampire can never have more votes, stealth, intercept or bleed than
it's current capacity. You may not play a card to increase a vampire's
votes, stealth, intercept or bleed above it's current capacity.

how's that? simple to remember, no maths required (unlike if the rule
was capacity/2 round down, or something annoying), and isn't a HUGE
change for a lot of decks. you could maybe include strength in the list,
for consistency. 'cause i guess 2, 3 or 4 strength is still nothing to
sneeze at when followed with a disarm, for those weenie pot lovers
amongst us. (hi peter! :D )

effects this would have that i can think of off the top of my head:

1 caps can't be prince/archbishop or 'greater' titles, only primogen,
bishops or prisci.

weenie vote will be harder to 'push' with (awe/bewitching), Awe on big
caps will also be a little more limited (if your IC already has 4 votes,
then the max you can awe for is 7...which is still a lot, but in line
with what some other people wanted to do to the card in the other thread).

Laz/Enkidu multirush still works fine :)

weenie dom watered down.

weenie kindred spirits still reasonably viable (but defenders will be
able to judge how much intercept they might need to save up, where
applicable, and know that the acting minion won't be able to go above a
certain stealth)

On Feb 12, 9:23 am, "Joshua Duffin" <joshduffin...@SPAM.gmail.com>
wrote:

> This is IMO because the advantages of smaller vampires are inherent in the
> game's mechanics (they cost less pool and have, consequentially, more
> actions-per-pool-invested, more blocks-per-pool-invested, and so on).
> Printing cards that help bigger vampires means you have to build your deck
> with, draw, and play the cards at the right times to gain whatever benefits
> they can provide. The smaller vampires have no such requirement to use
> their comparative advantages.

Barring library cards, I definitely agree that small vampires get more
actions-per-pool-invested and more blocks-per-pool-invested.

Nonetheless, every deck has library cards. By choosing to play with
big-cap vampires, you can get much more powerful effects, like Eternal
Vigilance, No Secrets, any of the cards that give blood to younger
uncontrolled vamps, any of the votes that help big vamps, the combo
discipline cards that tend to be more powerful, etc.

I do agree that when you choose to play big caps you have to ensure
they can act/block enough, but there are plenty of existing cards in
the game that allow such things (freak drive, forced march,
helicopter, wake varieties, etc.)

That said, I still think big caps could use a little more help, but I
don't think it's quite as dire as you make it out to be. I think the
weenie, mid-cap, big-cap decision creates interesting games and a
variety of playable decks, which is exactly what I want.

> Influence changes might do something, sure, but I think the action
> advantages over time are the bigger issue. Reducing small vampires'
> inherent bleed, votes, strength (or increasing the same for larger vampires,
> if you prefer) would be more apropos, I think.

I think influence changes would be a great idea, not only because it
helps big caps get out sooner and playing their cards, it also speeds
up the game in general (which would be a very significant plus!)
Timeouts and long games are significant detriments to fun play.

Regarding widespread rules changes related to capacity, haven't you
noticed that many big caps have inherent bonuses to bleed, strength,
intercept, stealth, and votes? The game is already balanced exactly
in the way you are suggesting.

Personally, I think LSJ is an incredible game designer for how well
this game has improved over time without a huge spike in the power
curve, all the while introducing new mechanics and allowing for a
diversity of strong deck types. It's really amazing!

Ira

>Then the weenies go off. Block the worst one (maybe after a bounce,
>plus a wake or Obedience or Cats' Guidance or *something* that
>reflects at least marginally competent deck-building) and you've
>handled a minimum of two, but probably three, maybe four. Next turn,
>four more transfers (barring something in your library to speed that
>along) and you have your second vampire (11 and 8, or 9 and 10). And so
>on.

Thing is, a weenie deck gets much better card cycling possibilities
early on. It can play a master card, just as the fattie deck can, and
both have a discard phase. But then it can take six actions, if it has
six minions, and throw away cards on each action to get to the good
stuff, if it's not got what it needs right now.

Most fattie decks can generate quite a bit of card cycling potential,
but it's usually not available early in the game - equipping a heart of
Nizchetus, getting out The Barrens (of which you might only have a
couple in the deck), breeding its own weenies (which can take several
turns), or whatever. But it can't sift through cards with anything like
as ruthless efficiency in the first couple of turns to get the defensive
wakes it needs. How many are in the deck to get maybe 2 or 3 in the
first hand? Let's say they're in the first 9 cards. 3 defensive cards
there, 90 card deck, so that's approximately 30 of various defensive
cards in the deck. That seems like a retrograde step for a fattie deck.

If we're considering marginally competent deck building, how many of
those weenie decks are going to include a Misdirection or an Anarch
Troublemaker? Not so useful at the moment, when a deck can be getting
out vampires much more slowly, but when it can get six out on the first
turn, that seems like a very different pay-off.

Now the deck throws down several Scouting Mission, Threats, Bonding etc.
(i.e. free bleeds, so they can go again next turn) If you can defend
against two, that still leaves 4 bleeds for, say, 3 - and potentially
throwing away useless cards on the blocked actions. Though with
something like Misdirection, I'm not sure you'd even necessarily be able
to defend against 2.

Unless the fattie deck gets a reasonably lucky shuffle (or, avoids a bad
shuffle), it looks like it won't be particularly happy.

I think it is intentional (well, for me it is) that weenie decks still
have it better under the proposed system. Just like with bleedzookas,
I think the presence of mono-discipline weenie decks is a *good* thing
in the game, mainly in terms of giving new players something they can
grasp easily and have a good shot at winning with. Weenie decks are
even better for this than stealth bleed, because if they screw up and
lose a nerd it doesn't really impact their game that much.

So it's OK that weenies still tend to be a better deal than fattie
decks, even under a much more generous influence system. The
individual nerds are more squishy and can accomplish less
individually, but more in aggregate. I don't want to see their
advantages disappear altogether. I just don't want them to be
egregious.

Messages.Author: bluedevil
Messages.Body:
On Feb 12, 12:02 pm, Johannes Walch <johannes.wa...@vekn.de> wrote:

> But this does not specifically the weenie problem, it just makes big-cap
> decks faster without the inclusion of speed-up master cards, but since
> it also speeds up weenie decks it doesn´t change much imho.

First, as things stand in a highly competitive environment, you need
to see that master card to enhance your influences, or you suffer
direly. Masters are the strongest cards in the game, and you are
eating a significant chunk of yours on something that still is
prayerish, and probably a dead card anytime after the first turn. So,
don't downplay not requiring those master cards. That in itself is a
significant balancing element.

Next, yes it's true, everybody speeds up. But as things stand,
weenies are "fast" and fatties are "slow". With the rising tide, you
get a new relationship of "fast" and "faster". That, to me, is moving
things in the proper direction.

> Example:
>
> Your predator influences 4 Ravnos Weenies in his 1st turn and play
> Parthenon. You influence Arika and Etrius (down to 8 pool)

I don't want to get too bogged down in specifics. I would suggest
trying it out and seeing if it breaks. You might be surprised, or you
might give us all (OK, me) some very valuable feedback. It's like
playtesting real sets.... it's easy to be an armchair genius and say
this or that is broken, but quite another thing to demonstrate it in
play.

But what I do want to comment on is "I influence out Arika and
Etrius". That is, probably, retarded. This system *will* give you
enough rope to hang yourself with, and it's a whole other dimension of
skill to know how to manage your now-unlimited transfers. The best
analogy that I have is an old pen and paper RPG called "Rolemaster".
Compared to other games at the time, this game gave low-level
characters these *huge* attack bonuses. But the combat system was
built with mechanics such that you allocated your defense for each
round of combat out of that same pool. So in that game, yes you
*could* throw everything into offense and go screaming forward, but it
would probably get you killed. Similarly for this system (although in
practice there are times when that is exactly what you want to do, and
reading the table and knowing when and where to do it is, like I said,
a skill. I like that).

C) If you want to slow down weenies dramatically, then include a
'scarcity' idea for all vampires. In other words, every time a new
vampire enters play (yes, even through creation rites, embrace, etc.,
but not temptation / from a sinking ship etc.), for each minion you
have beyond the first three, you must pay an extra pool to bring them
into play.

extra pool, the following one an extra 2 pool etc. This would
symbolise the extra amount of effort it takes a methuselah to control
that many vamps.

example, making it just cost an extra pool for every minion past the
second (1st 2 costs nothing, then all the rest cost 1 extra pool).

at any given time, so a weenie deck still has the advantage that it's

breeder decks, which I think many realise is a very powerful
archetype, whether it be the Brujah Debaters, !Torries el Grande, or
the Nightmarish Ravnos, or any other breeder deck.

anyway.

No more so than Taste of Vitae, which is disciplineless. The cost of a
card - and in this case a discipline - is not "no cost". Nor is it more
free than Perfectionist or Capitalist - you're going to take actions anyway,
why not gain blood while you're at it?

>> So are you going to fix all the other "totally broken" cases soon, too?
>> I don't care about slippery slopes but if you like fixing one thing that
>> you think is too powerful, why would you *not* fix all the other ones?
>
> So there are only two options: perfection or status quo?

There are two main options to one's *approach* to game balance: attempting
to achieve perfection (or at least come close to it), or conservatism
(sticking with the status quo except in extreme cases). If you are going to
attempt to achieve perfection, you should do so in many cases, not just a
few.

Josh

Let's see if I can have a try... Forgive me if I repeat a little bit.

Voter Captivation, as far as I can tell, has too much effect for a
single card. If it was just blood gain as an action modifier, that's
still a bit much. Pool gain as well is tending towards crazy. Art
Scam is 2 pool as an action. Sure, it may take a little bit more to
get a vote through. Perhaps one additional card. Art Scam will need
an action plus possibly some stealth. VC will need an action (a vote,
that is also damaging to your prey, and is "what your deck does", so
we don't count it as the additional card, because it accomplishes
other purposes besides gaining the pool), possibly some stealth, and
possibly a Bewitching Oration or an Awe. There, you've gained 2 pool,
plus possibly some blood, while not wasting an action because you also
did what your deck is designed to do. There are so many other cards
and actions to compare it to, but most of them have already been
visited and you're still not convinced. I understand that.

The other thing about Voter Captivation is that it has a profound, and
I emphasize profound, impact on the viability of vote decks. You
almost can't play a winning vote deck without VC... okay, don't go
into Lasombra voters/bleeders with Political Structure, etc... they
exist, but nearly to the degree of VC-supported vote. A good vote
deck with Voter Captivation, if not stopped early, will bloat like
crazy, using multiple minion taps, blood and pool from VC, bringing
out more vampires with votes with the extra pool, Minion Tapping and
Voter Capping with those minions, etc... It's a hideous cycle, all
fed by actions that still damage your prey at the same time. Admit
it, you've known the horror of watching a nasty vote deck bloating and
gearing up cross table with nothing you can do about it, right?
Admittedly, those decks don't utterly dominate the tournament scene,
but when they work, it is in HUGE part because of Voter Cap. And when
they do work, using VC, they're like a big cheesy boulder rolling down
a slick, buttery hillside... damn, I'm getting hungry. But, my point
is, these decks seem to start off in a very unstable equilibrium,
ready to push off to an early exit, or to a table sweeping at any
moment. And Voter Cap is the pressure pushing toward the table
sweep. *That* is why it is too powerful. I don't think you're
convinced, but I'll go on as though you are...

I don't think anyone has read any of my posts in this thread, but
early on, I mentioned that I wasn't sure Voter Cap needed to be
changed. But *something* should be done to balance its effect on the
game, because its effect is a bad one. In addition to being too
powerful, it also can make referendums excruciatingly annoying when
people have to balance their votes against a VC. And it can be
annoying even for political decks that don't use VC (as rare as those
are), because people will vote against you so you don't gain pool, and
then someone else will pull some surprise vote push to vote it down.

Obviously if Voter Cap were to be changed, there would have to be some
other force (or several forces) to push vote decks toward viability.
Because you guys are right that vote decks do have some costs
associated with them - big vampires, little stealth, table politics,
vote hosers... And Voter Cap is the crutch that offsets some of those
costs, and pretty much completely reverses the cost of having large
vamps. Or if Voter Cap is not changed, there have to be some viable
VC-hosers that are not also vote hosers (because why hose other voters
that don't even use the overpowered card?). Ideally, regardless of
what happens, there should be some more vote options for non-presence
disciplines, but that's more of a tangential thing, and not so much
part of the VC discussion.

i like this influence discussion. let me say how i'd like it to read
(and it could be an optional VEKN rule):

(regular influence rules) AND *first 2 turns a Meth has (2 full table
rounds) he or she may have unlimited transfers only to transfer to and
bring out 1 vampire/minion*

that way a weenie player who goes first gets neither benefit. they
already will catch up fast enough anyways, so not a big loss. also,
those extra influence type cards will still retain value in a variety of
decks. also, its KISS, which is crucial to prevent eyestrain for all.

i'd also like to offer a very naughty and evil suggestion, along the
lines of Temptation. i think that just because Meths influence doesn't
mean larger vampires don't. i think it might be interesting to explore a
new rule power for vampires 7+ capacity. how about this:

Vampires with capacity of 7 or more can take temporary control of a
vampire with a capacity of 2 or less. During the untap phase, the older
vampire gives blood to the target equal to its capacity (excess blood
goes to the blood bank, as normal) and takes control of this younger
vampire until the end of this turn. A vampire may do this more than once
per untap phase.

FYI: do not try to add tapping to the cost! the goal is to simply take
advantage of weenies ability to be easily bribed, used as pawns, in
general vampire politics. otherwise it'd be trading a big cap action for
a weenie action -- which equals waste of time! Temptation and Mind Rape
would still be solid because they'd be cheaper, last longer, or reach
larger targets. also, it would bring greater risk to playing weenies
because they would be easily manipulated by others, including your
predator. i don't know the full ramifications yet, but it's an
interesting start. also, because control is lost at the end of turn, if
you oust your weenie prey with his own weenies, those weenies will burn
after your turn ends, as per usual. this way you don't have to worry
about some bloating big cap player sweeping up all the weenies into some
30+ weenie end game army. there's quite a few benefits to this method, i
think...

Messages.Author: Andrew 'Wes' Weston
Messages.Body:
"atomweaver" <atomw...@hotmail.com> wrote

>
> THhe drawback of any library based solutions to big minion acceleration is
> that it must be incorporated in sufficient numbers so as to guarantee a
> draw in or near the game's opening, but those cards (ZIllah's Valley) are
> more useless as the game goes on, because you have sufficient influence by
> then.

Looking at the source material from which this game is derived, one of the
reasons why older vampires are more effective than younger ones is because
of their efficiency: while a younger vampire can typically burn 1 blood per
turn in the RPG, an elder can burn up to 3 blood per turn, all used to power
disciplines or pump strength, heal, whatever.

I'm not sure if I have suggested this here before or not, but here goes
(again, maybe):

Arbitrary Card Name
Unique Master
2 pool
Put this card in play. Once per turn, after performing a successful action,
any vampire with a capacity greater than 7 may burn 1 blood to untap at the
end of the turn. This card may be burned by any vampire with capacity above
7 as a (D) action.

(Could also be printed as an event, I guess)

So, basically a semi-permanent Mother of Horrors effect, allowing large
vampires (all at the table) to become more efficient while the card is in
play. I figure there've been enough untap effects added to the game lately
that haven't broken the game that we could afford to add one more.

Although any player using large vampires will likely be packing a copy of
the proposed card, they might not want to be the first one to play it.
Better to wait for someone else to play it, thus making them pay the 2 pool,
while still reaping the benefits yourself. On the other hand, the more decks
featuring large vampires at the table, the more likely this card will be
played sooner rather than later.

Note also that the card does not adversely affect weenie decks directly;
they just don't benefit from it.

Cheers,
WES

Now, there is a voice of reason. I agree wholeheartedly -- it is
foolhardy to look for "proof" for game design concepts like these.

Furthermore, jumping up and down and insisting that you be presented
with evidence to "prove" something that is so completely abstract and
judgement-laden demonstrates a total misunderstanding of the
complexity of the problem.

Let's look at a different, but perhaps equally complex issue, by way
of comparison. Can you "prove" that automobile exhaust and/or factory
emissions are the primary causes of global warming? No, you can't (as
the years of continuing debate have demonstrated), but that doesn't
mean that you can't make a judgement call and take action to reduce
emissions that clearly are having an impact. Or, conclude the other
way, for that matter, and continue to do as you will.

This, I think, is one reason behind LSJ's response that asks the folks
stomping their feet for "proof" to demonstrate the proof they have for
the "nope, it's not overpowered at all" side of the discussion. Said
proof has been equally un-forthcoming, equally un-proof-worthy, so
until you can do the impossible and "prove" that it isn't overpowered,

Or the strength VC gives to MT and Awe. Neither MT nor Awe are
problematic on their own. You could say that VC isn't problematic on
its own either, but the game is structured around spending blood to
pay for cards and heal damage. It's one of the basic premises of the
game. So cards that cost a lot of blood for a large advantage don't
strike me as unreasonable in that framework. But cards that give you
an arbitrary amount of blood back are problematic. You could take away
the cards that cost or move blood instead, but then we wouldn't really
be playing the same game anymore.

> Don't get me wrong, I love my MT and I don't want that banned either,
> however, I'm having a difficult time placing my finger on the EXACT
> problem (if any) here.

Massive amounts of blood gain cause issues, because one of the basic
premises of the game is that powerful effects cost blood. It's
significantly less problematic when it costs you forward momentum
(i.e., Renewed Vigor, Fifth Tradition) or is intensely limited
(Giant's Blood). It's not even been so bad on VC that the game has
been destroyed by it. But it does cause problems.

As has been *asserted* already. I don't see any posts where it was
convincingly demonstrated. Your arguments for Taste of Vitae being less
problematic than Voter Captivation appear to me to rest on Taste not
"negating" the cost of combat cards the way Voter Cap does the cost of
political actions/modifiers/etc (though that's your claim, not mine).
That's a card-design consideration, not a game-balance consideration, and
does not demonstrate that Taste of Vitae's blood gain is "less free" than
that from Voter Captivation.

>> card - and in this case a discipline - is not "no cost". Nor is it more
>> free than Perfectionist or Capitalist - you're going to take actions
>> anyway, why not gain blood while you're at it?
>
> It is moreso than those. See also master phase actions. And '1'.

No, those are equally free (cost a cardslot and the opportunity to play the
card), though you are correct that they don't grant as much blood
immediately when played. They may grant as much over the course of a game,
though, and do *not* rely on your deck succeeding in its task to give the
free blood (you just have to take successful actions for the archetypes, you
don't have to pass votes by X over the possible objections of other
players).

> The strength players find in Perfectionist, despite its shortcomings
> compared to Voter Captivation, is another case in the evidence column.

I'm sorry, it's really not. Players use Perfectionist because it's a good
effect; they use Voter Captivation because it's a good effect too. Its
relative shortcomings can't plausibly be counted as evidence against Voter
Captivation because it also has relative strengths, namely that it can be
used in any deck regardless of whether that deck can pass votes by X or has
Presence - those are very large relative advantages for Perfectionist
getting chosen in a lot of deck designs.

You can only count players' use of Perfectionist as evidence for Voter
Captivation being too strong if you can show that Voter Captivation is too
much stronger than Perfectionist - you have not yet even shown that it's
stronger at all (in the general case of designing decks that might want to
use one or the other of the two cards), let alone too much stronger.

>>>> that you think is too powerful, why would you *not* fix all the other
>>>> ones?

>>

>> attempting to achieve perfection (or at least come close to it), or
>> conservatism (sticking with the status quo except in extreme cases). If
>> you are going to attempt to achieve perfection, you should do so in many
>> cases, not just a few.
>
> You might want to check with Zopf about that.

I'm not sure what objection you are making to my points on how a designer
may approach game balance by pointing to Mr. Zopf here. If you're arguing
against that claim, would you mind putting forth an actual argument against
it? It's difficult for me to psychically guess what I need to convince you
of. :-)

As far as I can see, there is a real cost to players every time a card text
is changed. It should not be done lightly. However, if one is going to
take the other approach to designing the game, logically one ought to aim
for greater perfection in all of the game's cards, not just a few at a time.

Does it? I'm not so sure. It seems that the consequence of a VC which is
overpowered enough to warrant changing would be somewhat apparent in
tournament results (ie. there'd be evidence). The only things anyone came
up with in this thread towards that end was Peter citing 6 vote-centric
decks winning in the last 20 tournaments in the TWDA, and the script which
collected the instances of use of cards.

If I'm looking at the same decks as Peter, they are

a Guruhi Deck (no VC)
an Ishtarri/ Obf-Pre Sabbat deck (8 VC)

have 1-4 political actions (usually parity shifts), but no VC there,
either...

Thats not conclusive evidence, but its the sort of analysis that is
helpful.

> Let's look at a different, but perhaps equally complex issue, by way
> of comparison.

I don't like analogies. Can't we just talk about the topic at hand?

> Can you "prove" that automobile exhaust and/or factory
> emissions are the primary causes of global warming? No, you can't

Sure, but you can amass enough evidence such that it would be "perverse to
withhold provisional assent"*

http://www.ipcc.ch/SPM2feb07.pdf

> (as the years of continuing debate have demonstrated),

Political debate != lack of Scientific concensus

> but that doesn't
> mean that you can't make a judgement call and take action to reduce
> emissions that clearly are having an impact. Or, conclude the other
> way, for that matter, and continue to do as you will.
>
> This, I think, is one reason behind LSJ's response that asks the folks
> stomping their feet for "proof" to demonstrate the proof they have for
> the "nope, it's not overpowered at all" side of the discussion. Said
> proof has been equally un-forthcoming, equally un-proof-worthy, so
> until you can do the impossible and "prove" that it isn't overpowered,
> doesn't it seem rather brash to command others to do what you cannot?
>

"Proof", in the manner in which you're using it here, is for mathematics
and philosophical exercises in logic, not science, and not games. But
where you are wrong in your analogy is that "proof" is not what is being
asked for. If someone asserts "VC is overpowered" and another says "prove
it", or "show me", what they're really asking for is evidence for the
assertion. Evidence is what we use to inform our decisions, and if there
is enough of it, we can change our minds on VC (or Global Warming).

If VC is overpowered, it would stand to reason that you could check for the
consequences of its being overpowered. One check would be that overpowered
cards tend to be noticed by the talented players worldwide, leveraged for
tournament wins, and thus show a unbalanced presence in the TWDA, or if it
were overpowered in a manner which was disruptive, one would expect that
people would vocalize aobut the need to include special defenses in
planning for opponent's use of the card. Thus far, there is no evidence
for VC being overpowered, in terms of high tournament win results, or in
terms of a need for special defense. There could be other checks (tests)
which would provide evidence that VC is overpowered, but those are the only
two which come to mind right now.

DaveZ

The answer is (D), but you need to add in, uh, (C.5?) which is "this all
happens while your deck is killing your prey, too" (i.e. Voter Cap
happens as you KRC or Parity Shift or PTO, as opposed to Renewed Vigor
or 5th or Concert Tour, all of which only happen when you take a
specific action to use them which is not also killing your prey).

> If it's A. Renewed Vigor does the same thing. Will this be next to
> consider? (just asking)

Unlikely. As it is a blood gaining specific action. That comes with a
very specific, high cost (you need superior Salubritude which only comes
on 2 vampires per grouping, and they are scarce). The cost of Voter Cap
is "doing what you were doing anyway, and killing your prey at the same
time".

> If it's B. you must push votes and have PRE. Strong, but
> overpowered???? Not sold.

If you are playing a presence vote deck, you have PRE. And you were
pushing the votes anyway.

> If it's C. then again I assert that Minon Tap is the criminal here.
> VC is mearly the conduit to bloats end. But so is RV and old 5th.

Minion Tap is a card with a high payoff that comes with a high cost. The
problem comes from Minion Tapping and then refilling for little to no
effort (while killing your prey at the same time), not from simply
Minion Tapping. If you tap Arika for 10, great, you have 10 more pool,
but Arika only has 1 blood. Which makes her very vulnerable. If you can
then refill Arika with limited effort (while killing your prey at the
same time), the cost of the Minion Tap ceases to be that significant.

> I understand it's a design issue as well, but again, is that because
> of the strengh MT gives to VC. Or is it that Awe lets you basicly auto
> pass your vote to fill again, rinse and repeat.

Both Minion Tap and Awe are totally reasonable in and of themselves
(i.e. powerful cards with very significant costs). Introduce Voter Cap,
and their significant costs become much, much less significant.

Taste is equally limited by the capacity of the tasting minion.

> and you must generate x "in favor" votes above
> whats needed to pass, of course.

X votes in favor can typically be generated more easily than a) making
sure the opposing minion has X blood on them plus b) making sure they
lose X blood due to damage in a single round of combat - especially
since giving them more blood to fulfill a) runs counter-purpose to
most combat decks. I'm not really sure how I could go about "proving"
this statement, but I'm pretty sure it's generally true. Not to
mention that entering combat is generally more dangerous than calling
a vote.

> Is it the +2 pool which bothers you?
> Because thats the only thing I see above and beyond what limits both
> cards.

Taste does not create blood from nowhere. It has to be on the opposing
minion, then lost by them due to damage in combat. If your minion goes
to torpor, the blood is lost. If the opposing minion burns blood in
some way other than damage, the Taste is less effective. If the
opponent just has weenie vampires (or chump blocks with one) your
Taste is less effective. VC puts new blood (and pool) on the table,
limited only by the number of votes you can generate and the capacity
of the acting minion.

> But then, Taste is discipline-less, anyone can use it... The
> nerfing of Pulled Fangs and Embrace would indicate a general trend
> towards discipline-less cards having the lesser effect.

Sure. That doesn't mean that the greater effect is automatically
balanced.

>

> cards.jyhad/msg/eb91dca4e6079fb4?dmode=source&hl=en

> say it is _not_the blessing I thought it was five years ago. Its just
> another set of problems/complications that need to be clarified, which
> is why I'd rather we would all just be done with meddling with card
> text, altogether. Its a lot easier to "sell" card text changes to a new
> player if you can say that there are no more coming with a degree of
> honesty. "

I'll come out and say I don't know whether VC is overpowered enough to
warrant change. But I think it's pretty clearly one of the more
powerful effects in the game, and I think it probably has a negative
impact on the design process. While it may appear that I'm arguing for
it being changed, that's not really the case. I just think that most
of the "it's fine, don't change it" arguments (besides this one) are
pretty flawed, and it's in my nature to point out those flaws.

So I don't know what the right answer really is. I *do* hope that LSJ
takes the burden on players into consideration. But I don't think we
can reasonably expect him not to make occasional tweaks for the good
of the game - it's practically inevitable that the errata/rulings/
migrations list will grow over time. I hope that it does so slowly and
only after careful consideration. This seems to have been the case in
recent history (and in more distant history, it seems the problems
were drastic enough to justify the drastic measures taken at the
time).

> Regards
> DaveZ
> atom weaver

Ah. You see, most of those happened quite a long time ago, and it was my
impression that White Wolf intended not to continue altering card-texts in
such a carefree fashion. For the very sensible reason that it should
require a pretty substantial problem with a card to justify altering its
text and making all the extant copies incorrect. And that if you're going
to go out and fix lots of overpowered cards, one would expect the fixing to
extend to everything that needed fixing. (ie, if Voter Captivation were
going to be changed, I would have expected to see it changed in CE along
with Fifth Tradition, Taste of Vitae, and Day Operation.)

Speaking of Day Operation, by the way, I was astounded that that change got
made. A card that had been in print since Jyhad, changed to not work
against allies because of... flavor reasons? It boggles the mind.
Certainly Day Op wasn't particularly overpowered as written; as revised, it
is very nearly wallpapered by Daring the Dawn.

To my mind, if one wants to open up the universe of possible card designs
for new sets, the really logical thing to do at this point, rather than
picking out individual existing cards and changing their texts around, is to
embrace full-on set rotation. You already did it for that very reason with
vampires through the grouping rules; if old library cards are now
problematic for allowing the design of new library cards, why not start
rotating the legal sets for library cards too? It would instantly solve the
problem of Voter Captivation (not to mention about a hundred other "top of
the power curve" cards including the ones Ben Swainbank recently pointed to
as limiting competitive deck design).

Granted, this idea doesn't seem to be all that popular with the player-base.
But changing individual card-texts isn't very popular with the player-base
either.

Josh

> no logical imperative to pay all the costs up front. If doing so
> brings in some tangible benefit, put that on the table and so that we
> can discuss whether it's worth the cost.

John, I respect your arguments, but this is a terrible analogy. :-)
Cardtext changes are not consumed one at a time with a limit as to how many
you can "enjoy" in a single day. In fact, if a cardtext change is going to
benefit you, the more of them you can have immediately, the longer you'll
have for them all to give you their benefits. It is *absolutely* best to
get all the cardtext changes at once if you're going to get them eventually:
you have fewer wrongly-printed cards in circulation, you don't have to keep
telling players "oh, now this card has changed too", you can tell players
that the problems have all been fixed already so now they won't have to
worry much about new problems cropping up down the road.

If you see what I'm getting at, with card-text changes, there's supposed to
be a net *benefit* to players every time one is made. If there is a cost to
making the change, it's supposed to be outweighed by the benefits. So when
you're getting benefits, you get the *most* benefit by getting as many
benefits as possible as soon as you can.

Josh

better to wait until we've analyzed every card that is under
consideration for change before changing any of them? What happens if
something crops up that changes our analysis of a given card after we
claim that we've fixed all the problem cards?

If it were plainly obvious when cards warranted change, you'd be
absolutely correct. But the existence of this thread pretty much
squashes that idea. So the question becomes, do we wait until we've
analyzed all potential problem cards and determined which ones are
worth fixing? Or do we analyze them one at a time and get those net
benefits in circulation sooner?

> Josh

> needs a new benefits package

Howdy,

> I would buy that. I mean, it'd be something. I think allowing 2-caps to
> bleed for 2 and 3-caps to bleed for 3 (at 2 and 3 stealth respectively)

> limit "damage inflicted in a round" or something like that, since if
> "strength" were the only limited factor, weenie CEL guns wouldn't be
> affected, but weenie POT combat would.

So Rico's Bombs would only do 2? What, he only knows where to find
pipe bombs? It wouldn't make much sense that weenies couldn't make
equipment work right, while fatties (and allies) presumably still
could.

I see no real reason to put capacity restrictions on combat; using low
capacity vampires is one of the only ways you can make combat go at
all right now. (And weenie guns is generally laying out enough pool
per vampire that it's really 'mid-cap' guns by the time it's done.) I
suppose that if you wanted to make a rule that _permanent_ strength
(or votes or stealth or intercept or bleed) couldn't be larger than
capacity, that would be OK, though Smudge won't like it.

Personally, I like the schemes where base values (really, just bleed
and maybe votes) are keyed to capacity, so that small vampires have 0
base bleed, while big ones have +1 or even +2 bleed. And even if you
made it apply to strength (which I wouldn't advocate), 0 base strength
wouldn't make a huge amount of difference to most weenie combat.

Alex

If you want to get fancy, you could salvage this by introducing "debut" tokens:
A Methuselah gets 1 Debut token every influence phase. Unused debut tokens are
kept from turn to turn (unlike transfers -- hey, that's why they're tokens).

Then redefine the influence phase activity:
1 transfer -> 1 blood on (unchanged)
2 transfers -> 1 blood off (unchanged)
4 transfers + 1 pool + 1 debut token -> draw from crypt to uncontrolled.
at end: burn debut tokens to move "full" minions to controlled (at one debut
token per minion).

That is, moving a crypt card during the influence phase costs a debut token.

(with or without the rule making it mandatory to do so if you have a debut token
and a full vampire).
